docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
MajorDom consists of several key components: devices, hub, cloud, bridge, mobile application, and voice assistant.

Devices play a crucial role in the system as they enable control over physical parts of the home. They communicate using radio modules and the “Merlin” protocol that receive commands from the hub, and transmit events back to it.

The hub is the central element of the system. It manages the devices and coordinates their operations. The hub holds the main database with information about users, home, rooms, and devices. Through a local HTTP server and WS server, the hub provides an API for interacting with the database and for high-level control of devices.

The cloud is the server-side component and plays a vital role in user authentication. It stores the database of users, homes, hubs, and their access rights. Device models with a list of parameters and a firmware update system are also stored in the cloud.

The bridge is a WS server that provides communication between the hub and remote user over the internet. It enables sending commands and receiving information from the hub without being within the home's local network.

The system can have multiple bridges located in different places. Clients select the nearest or least loaded bridge to minimize communication delays.

One of the main features of the MajorDom is its fault tolerance. Despite the collapse of one or multiple bridges, the system perseveres and maintains its functionality. The remaining available bridges take on the tasks of the inactive bridges, ensuring uninterrupted data exchange between the hub and clients.

Even a complete loss of internet connection on the hub is not a problem. All the logic and command processing occur locally, ensuring independence from the internet connection and maintaining the ability to control devices within the local network. However, such scenarios are rare since the hub can be simultaneously connected via Wi-Fi and an Ethernet cable, and future support for cellular network will be added.

Smart home control is achieved through a mobile application that provides a user-friendly interface. However, in practice, the role of the mobile application often reduces to system configuration, while day-to-day device management is carried out using automatic scenarios and the voice assistant.

Like the hub, the voice assistant can work completely offline, ensuring security, privacy, and reliability of use.

docs.title: Create a Custom Device Model
docs.text:
1. Open the MajorDom mobile app.
  2. Navigate to Settings and enable Developers Mode.
  3. Return to the home screen and tap the + button located in the top-right corner.
  4. Alongside the existing options "Create a Room" and "Add a Device", a new option, "Create a Device Model", will now be available.
  5. Choose Create a Device Model.
  6. Provide a name for your custom device model and define a set of parameters. Custom parameters can also be added.
  7. After creation, the device model and its parameters will be stored on the Hub.
  8. You can now use this custom device model with new devices in your home by specifying the device model UUID in the sketch and implementing parameter handling.

docs.title: Merlin24 C++
docs.text:
Merlin24 works with low-power, long-range nrf24l01 radio modules operating on the 2.4GHz band.

Here's an example sketch for controlling a relay:

#include <Merlin24.h>

// Define pin numbers
#define RELAY_PIN 3
#define BUTTON_PIN 4

// Variables to store the state
byte relay_state = LOW;
byte last_button_state = HIGH; // Assuming pull-up

// Define constants for function codes
#define RELAY_PARAMETER 1

// Initialize Merlin24 object with device model uuid and parameter value handler function
Merlin24 device("10359220-c504-40d0-bed7-f254cc85e75c", [](byte parameter_index, byte value) {
    switch (parameter_index) {
        case RELAY_PARAMETER:
            // toggle the relay and save new state
            relay_state = value;
            digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, value);
            break;
        // You can add more cases here for other parameters
        default:
            break; // Handle unknown function code here (optional)
    }
});

void setup() {
    pinMode(RELAY_PIN, OUTPUT);
    pinMode(BUTTON_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);
}

void loop() {
    /*
        tick() is required for Merlin24 to work
        it should be called as often as possible
        avoid delays and other blocking code
    */
    device.tick();

    /* 
        Toggle the relay on the button press
        Just an example, in real life you would probably want to debounce the button
    */

    // Read the button state
    byte current_button_state = digitalRead(BUTTON_PIN);

    // Check for button press (LOW when pressed because of pull-up resistor)
    if (last_button_state == HIGH && current_button_state == LOW) {

        // Toggle the relay, save the state and send it to hub
        digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, relay_state);
        relay_state = !relay_state;
        device.send(RELAY_PARAMETER, relay_state);
    }

    // Update last button state
    last_button_state = current_button_state;
}

docs.title: MerlinWiFi (MerlinHttp) C++
docs.text:
The MerlinHttp class provides a way to connect your device to a hub over HTTP, making it a great choice for devices that require internet access or advanced capabilities. It is particularly suitable for ESP32/ESP8266 boards.

To switch from Merlin24 to MerlinHttp, all you need to do is change the included header and initialize MerlinHttp instead. In most cases, this should be sufficient.

#include <MerlinHttp.h>
// ... (other parts remain unchanged)
MerlinHttp device("10359220-c504-40d0-bed7-f254cc85e75c", [](byte parameter_index, byte value) {
// ... (other parts remain unchanged)

docs.title: Manually (MerlinHttp Protocol Overview)
docs.text: If you want to use other technologies, hardware, or software—e.g., a Raspberry Pi with a Python program and FastAPI server—you can still communicate with the Hub over HTTP by implementing the required endpoints manually. Below is an overview of how the Hub-to-Device and Device-to-Hub communication occurs.

docs.title: Hub-to-Device Communication
docs.text:
Your device should host an HTTP server and expose the following RESTful API endpoints:

GET /api/v1/merlin: Used by the Hub to get current device state Reponse Payload: 

[
    {
    "index": "<parameter_index: int in 0...255>",
    "value": "<parameter_value: base64 encoded value>"
    },
]

POST /api/v1/merlin: Used by the Hub to send parameter updates to the device.

Request Payload: 

{
"index": "<parameter_index: int in 0...255>",
"value": "<parameter_value: base64 encoded value>"
}

POST /api/v1/credentials: Used by the Hub to send network and authentication credentials to the device on initial setup.

Request Payload: 

{
"ssid": "<Wi-Fi SSID>",
"psk": "<Wi-Fi Password>",
"hub_host": "<Hub Host Address>",
"token": "<JWT Token>"
}

docs.title: Device-to-Hub Communication
docs.text:
To communicate with the Hub, the device should make HTTP requests to the Hub's API endpoints:

Send Parameter Updates: {hub_host}/api/merlin/state

Request Payload: 

{
"index": "<parameter_index: int in 0...255>",
"value": "<parameter_value: base64 encoded value>"
}

Update Device Host (ip:port) Address: {hub_host}/api/merlin/host

Request Payload: 

{
"host": "<device_host_address>"
}

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Authentication is implemented using a long-lived JWT token included in the Authorization header of each HTTP request:

"Authorization": "Bearer <JWT Token>"

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: To make a device discoverable, setup zeroconf service of type _majordom-device._tcp and specify the port of the merlin interface server. Now Hub can find the device in your LAN.

docs.title: Parameter (Value) Types
docs.text:
Current available types:

class ParameterType(str, Enum):
    # Base types
    integer = "integer"  # uint8
    decimal = "decimal"  # uint8 casting from [0, 255] to [0, 1]
    boolean = "boolean"  # real one-bit integer
    enum = "enum"        # uint8 with string_representation
    string = "string"    # string

    humidity = "humidity"          # decimal;
    temperature = "temperature"    # float8;
    color_temperature = "color_temperature"  # Kelvin, decimal; 0.5 is white
    rgb = "rgb"                    # hue wheel angle, decimal; TODO: uint8[3];
    volume = "volume"              # decimal;
    timeinterval = "timeinterval"  # seconds, int32;

    button = "button"              # None, just a button

Example of decoding:

class DeviceParameter(Parameter): # pydantic.BaseModel
    value: bytes

    class Config:
        json_encoders = {
            bytes: lambda v: base64.b64encode(v).decode()
        }

    @validator('value', pre=True)
    def base64_decode(cls, value: str) -> bytes:
        if value is not None and isinstance(value, str):
            return base64.b64decode(value)
        return value

    @property
    def decoded_value(self) -> int | float | bool | str | bytes:
        match self.value_type:

            case ParameterType.integer | ParameterType.enum:
                return max(0, min(int.from_bytes(self.value, 'big'), 255)) # int as uint8 in [0, 255]

            case ParameterType.timeinterval:
                return int.from_bytes(self.value, 'big') # just int

            case ParameterType.decimal | ParameterType.humidity | ParameterType.temperature | ParameterType.color_temperature | ParameterType.rgb | ParameterType.volume:
                return max(0, min(int.from_bytes(self.value, 'big'), 255)) / 255 # float in [0, 1] mapped from uint8 in [0, 255]

            case ParameterType.boolean:
                return bool(self.value[0])

            case ParameterType.string:
                return self.value.decode('utf-8') # utf-8 is default but explicit is better than implicit

            case ParameterType.button:
                return b'\x00'

            case _:
                return self.value

docs.title: MajorDom Device Integration Guide
docs.text:
Under active development

MajorDom is still under development. The integration structure is now stable, but implementation details are still subject to change.

An integration is a standalone Python package that bridges MajorDom Hub with IoT devices of a specific protocol or vendor (e.g. HomeKit, Zigbee, Z-Wave). It depends only on the published majordom-integration-sdk — not on the Hub source — so it can be developed, tested, and even run on its own.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Don't start from a blank folder. Every integration is scaffolded from the integration-template repository: click Use this template → Create a new repository, name it integration-<protocol>, and follow the template README's checklist (rename the placeholder package to majordom_<protocol>, poe install, wire up CI and PyPI publishing). The template ships a working example controller, tests, and CI, so you replace pieces rather than assemble them from scratch. This guide explains the concepts behind that code.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text:
The SDK and the integration template are released under the Apache License 2.0: use them freely, for MajorDom integrations or in your own projects, including library mode. We do ask you to keep what you build on them open source.

Most official integrations are source-available for noncommercial use. For a commercial license, contact us — we're open to partnership: https://parker-industries.org/partnership.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Term Meaning Hub The MajorDom Hub core software Integration A protocol/vendor-specific plugin Peripheral Anything that needs or provides capabilities: a radio, a service, an in-process provider, the integration's controller itself. See Peripherals Need Something external a peripheral requires: a radio, a server, or a discovery provider (ZEROCONF, UPNP_SSDP, BLE_ROUTER). The runtime binds it and hands it over in self.peripherals Discovery Service A provider the runtime runs in-process (Zeroconf, SSDP, or the Bluetooth router) that fires raw discovery events. Needed like any other, see Discovery Services Controller (capitalized) The class your integration must implement (AbstractController subclass) a controller (lowercase) Any third-party device that can control IoT devices (smartphone, Alexa, etc.) Discovery A detected, unpaired device that is available to be paired Device A paired and controllable device saved in the Hub's database Parameter A single controllable or observable property of a device (e.g. brightness, temperature)

A device moves through these states:

Invisible → Discoverable (Discovery) → Paired (Device)

docs.title: Suggested Module Structure
docs.text:
Your integration is its own package, majordom_<protocol>/ (the template starts you with this — integration_template/ renamed). An integration will typically need more than just a controller. Recommended minimal layout:

majordom_myintegration/
├── __init__.py          # exports peripherals(platform): the controller and the services it brings
├── controller.py        # AbstractController subclass — the only required implementation; discovery callbacks and cancel closures are typically stored here too
├── models.py            # Typed integration_data schemas for Device and Parameter subclasses, see Storing Data
├── mapper.py            # Protocol ↔ MajorDom domain model conversions, isolated from the controller for readability
└── parameters_map.py    # Supplemental metadata for parameters that the API does not expose, usually in a form of a static dictionary. For example, device might expose min/max limits for a number via device's API, but the unit is only defined in pdf specification.

controller.py is the only required implementation. The rest are a template for keeping the controller clean — separate models, pull out conversion logic into a mapper, add metadata dictionary, etc. Of course, other files can be added as needed.

docs.title: Implementation Checklist
docs.text:
Track it in your repo: the integration template README ships this and the Quality Checklist as a fillable copy — tick items there as you implement them. The list below is the reference.

  • [ ] Discovery registered with the providers it needs — self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF), UPNP_SSDP and/or BLE_ROUTER as appropriate; cancel closures saved and called in stop
  • [ ] Discovery listeners fire when devices are found, and the controller calls self.output.controller_did_receive_discovery
  • [ ] Every reachable paired device reported on start (self.output.controller_did_connect_device(self, physical_id=...)): the Hub marked them all unavailable when the integration stopped
  • [ ] start_pairing_window is implemented if the protocol requires an explicit scan mode
  • [ ] Device pairing (pair_device is implemented, and validates the incoming ProvidedCredentials.type against discovery.expected_credentials_options before using it; fills the draft it is given and returns it, without using the repository or reporting the device; sets physical_id and calls check_device_id once it is known, never changes the Hub's id)
  • [ ] Device schema is properly mapped: device info, parameter list, and each parameter's metadata are translated to MajorDom's domain model
  • [ ] Hub → Device control (send_command is implemented)
  • [ ] Device → Hub event subscription (self.output.controller_did_receive_events is called on incoming events)
  • [ ] identify, unpair, and fetch are implemented: unpair also rolls back a failed or unsaved pairing (any partial state, reverse order, only what blocks a re-pair, no waiting for the user, safe to call again) and raises DeviceUnreachableError when the device can't be reached; pair_device sets identity only, fetch returns the whole device with its parameters (or None when it doesn't answer); both are idempotent (check the device, re-subscribe only if the subscription is gone, bounded time)
  • [ ] Paired devices going offline/coming back online while the Hub is running (not just on reboot) — set device.available accordingly, and clear/set last_error to match
  • [ ] Graceful shutdown in stop
  • [ ] Everything external declared as a Need — radios, BLE_ROUTER, ZEROCONF, UPNP_SSDP, the services it brings; never raw Bluetooth
  • [ ] Bound needs read from self.peripherals, host facts and storage from self.platform, reports sent through self.output
  • [ ] Integration-level problems reported with a stable error id (IntegrationError) and resolved when they clear
  • [ ] Quality: once it's functional, the integration meets the Quality Checklist — reliability, tests, and maintainability — before release

See Implementing a Controller for details, or Example Integration for a narrative walkthrough of the template's controller. The template README mirrors this checklist as its Progress list, so you can track your integration against it directly in your repo.

docs.title: Running standalone
docs.text:
You don't need a running Hub to develop an integration. The SDK ships a dev runner that binds your controller's needs through the SDK runtime, as the Hub does (the Bluetooth router, Zeroconf, SSDP, radios and services), gives it a local repository, starts it, and logs everything it discovers:

import asyncio
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import run_controller
import majordom_myintegration

asyncio.run(run_controller(majordom_myintegration.peripherals))

It needs the runtime extras: pip install "majordom-integration-sdk[runtime,ble,discovery]". Pass db_path=... to persist devices across restarts (a file-backed SQLite repository) instead of the default in-memory one. See Standalone Mode for the interactive CLI, build_platform for your own scripts, and running without Docker or radios.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Integrations run their tests against a virtual/simulated device where possible, so CI doesn't need physical hardware. The SDK's majordom_integration_sdk.testing module provides the doubles: build_test_platform() wires a RecordingControllerOutput, an in-memory repository and temp-dir storage, and FakeZeroconf, FakeSSDP, FakeBLERouter (with FakeBLESources) and FakeOffers stand in for the peripherals, so a test can drive your controller and assert on what it reported. The template's tests/ show the pattern. (Real-hardware validation lives in the Hub, not in the integration package.)

docs.title: For IP Devices
docs.text:
• Handle IP changes. DHCP can reassign addresses. Identify devices by a stable ID (MAC, serial, mDNS hostname, domain-provided id) rather than IP. Monitor ip address regularly and keep it up to date.
  • Use the Hub's provided discovery. Need ZEROCONF, UPNP_SSDP or BLE_ROUTER and register through self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF).register(...). See Discovery Services. Do not run your own discovery stack.

docs.title: For all code
docs.text:
• No hand-typed keys: if a typo breaks it, type it. Static keys and formatted strings come from typed names, never from a bare string literal repeated where they're used:
    • the SDK's typed needs, BLE_ROUTER, ZEROCONF and UPNP_SSDP, read back with self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER);
    • SettingsExtraField for settings fields: Field(11, json_schema_extra={Extra.read_only: True});
    • ComposeService for a service's compose definition;
    • your own enum or constant for anything else.
  • Ids come from one helper each. Derive device and parameter ids through the SDK helpers or one function of your own, never a format string repeated across the code. It's the same rule as above: a typo makes a second id, and state and automations stop matching.
  • Error messages and other text meant for people stay plain strings.

docs.title: Implementing a Controller
docs.text:
Start from the template

Scaffold your integration from the integration-template (Use this template → Create a new repository), and read the Example Integration walkthrough alongside this page — it puts every piece below together in one worked controller.

docs.title: AbstractController Overview
docs.text:
Your integration's controller subclasses AbstractController from the SDK. It is generic over your Device and Parameter subclasses, your settings model, and the model of the draft a pairing fills (the last two are optional):

from majordom_integration_sdk.controller import AbstractController
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas import Device, Parameter

class MyController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    name = "My Protocol"  # optional — auto-derived from the class name ("My") otherwise
    ...

The full form is AbstractController[TDevice, TParameter, TSettings, TDeviceState]. TSettings defaults to Any and TDeviceState to DeviceState. To type the draft, write Any in the settings slot if you have none, and override device_state_type (see Storing Data).

docs.title: The name and key identity
docs.text:
name is a class attribute, shown to the user. It defaults to the class name without Controller (HueController → "Hue"):

class MyController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    name = "Hue"

Its slug is the controller's key ("hue"). The Hub knows the integration by its key: its devices (Device.integration), settings, documents folder, DISABLE_SERVICES and /integrations/{key}/…. Never rename name once released.

docs.title: The entry point
docs.text:
The integration package exports peripherals(platform): the controller and the services it brings along. The Hub calls it with its Platform.

def peripherals(platform: Platform) -> list[Peripheral]:
    return [matterjs_server(), MatterController(platform)]

docs.title: Hub → Device
docs.text: Implement all abstract methods defined in AbstractController — start, stop, pair_device, unpair, identify, fetch, send_command, and the discoveries property. The Hub calls these to drive your integration.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
The Hub pairs a device in two steps: your pair_device fills a draft, then the Hub saves it. No device record exists while pair_device runs.

async def pair_device(
    self, discovery: Discovery, draft: DeviceState, credentials: ProvidedCredentials | None
) -> DeviceState: ...

The Hub builds draft from what the user entered in the app: name, room, icon, category, note. Its id is the Hub's own and read-only: never change it. Its physical_id holds the discovery's id as a placeholder, and integration is your key. When the user picks an existing record to pair onto, the draft carries that record's data instead, its id, physical_id and integration_data included. The integration decides what in it is stale.

You establish the device's identity and trust only: its physical_id, integration_data (keys, addresses), available. Then you return the draft. The Hub saves it, reports the device connected if it is available, and calls fetch, which gives the device its parameters. So, during pair_device:

  • Don't use the device repository. Nothing is saved while pairing.
  • Report nothing about this device. No controller_did_connect_device, no events. The Hub reports after it saved the draft.
  • Check the physical id early. As soon as you know it, call check_device_id (below), before anything irreversible: it confirms no other record holds this device already.
  • Fill integration_data before each irreversible step. A key you are about to set, a node you are about to include: write it to the draft first. It is saved with the device, so you need no storage of your own. If pairing fails, the Hub calls unpair(draft) to roll back, and unpair can only undo what the draft says ran.
  • Just raise on failure. The Hub's unpair(draft) undoes the partial pairing.
  • Don't map parameters, read values or subscribe. Leave parameters empty: the Hub calls fetch for all of that right after the save.
  • Be idempotent. The user may retry after a failed or rolled-back attempt, with a fresh draft. Bring the device to a known-good paired state from whatever the last attempt left: check each step and redo only what is missing or stale. A device found already paired is confirmed and returned, not refused.
  • Raise when you can't pair. Raise MissingCredentialsError before touching the device when the Hub lacks credentials.
async def pair_device(self, discovery, draft, credentials):
    if not discovery.accepts(credentials):
        raise ValueError("Unsupported or missing credentials for this discovery")
    serial = await self._client.read_serial(discovery.id)                   # pseudo, read-only
    draft.physical_id = self.device_uuid(serial)
    await self.check_device_id(draft.physical_id, draft)                    # before anything irreversible
    draft.integration_data = AcmeDeviceIntegrationData(device_key=new_key)  # before the step it describes
    await self._client.pair(discovery.id, key=new_key)                      # pseudo, irreversible
    draft.available = True
    return draft

docs.title: check_device_id
docs.text:
@final
async def check_device_id(self, physical_id: UUID, draft: TDeviceState): ...

Optional, but call it. It raises DeviceIdTakenError when another record holds physical_id, the one you are giving the device. The record the user picked to pair onto (draft.id) is not another. The Hub refuses the pairing with that error and does not roll it back, because nothing ran.

from majordom_integration_sdk.errors import DeviceIdTakenError

error: DeviceIdTakenError
error.physical_id # the id in question
error.device_id   # the Hub id of the record that holds it
error.name        # the name of the record that holds it
error.is_paired   # False: a record kept after its device was removed

The app uses the record's name and is_paired to offer pairing onto that record instead.

docs.title: Device ids
docs.text:
A device has two ids:

  • id is the Hub's. The Hub assigns it, and you never change it.
  • physical_id is yours: what you look the device up by, in the repository (repo.get(physical_id=...)), in events and in controller_did_connect_device(self, physical_id=...). Build it with device_uuid(s), where s is a string or bytes unique to that device: a MAC address or a serial number. Build it in one place, a single id-making method, never assembled anew at each call site. A name or an address two devices share gives them the same id, and the second one can't be paired. Never change the physical_id of a device that is already paired.

docs.title: unpair is also the rollback
docs.text:
async def unpair(self, device: TDevice): ...

The user triggers it to remove a device. The Hub also calls it to roll back, with the draft as pair_device left it, at any stage: when pair_device raises anything but DeviceIdTakenError, and when the Hub fails to save what it returned. So:

  • Undo everything pairing did, in reverse order: a key set on the device, the pairing it holds, its place on the network or fabric.
  • Tolerate any partial state: a placeholder physical_id, no integration_data, a device already reset.
  • Never wait for the user. Go as far as you can: it is best effort, and the Hub cuts it off after 30 seconds.
  • Make it safe to call again. On a device already unpaired, or never fully paired, it does nothing more.

Talk to the device only: the Hub alone decides whether to delete the record and its integration_data. When the device can't be reached, raise DeviceUnreachableError and change nothing else.

The user sees the original pairing error, not an error from the rollback. When the rollback can't reach the device, the Hub answers pairing_failed: "Pairing failed. The device may need a manual factory reset to pair again."

docs.title: Removing a device
docs.text:
The app removes a device with DELETE /device/{id}?mode=...:

mode What happens unpair calls unpair, keeps the record delete (default) calls unpair, then removes the record forget removes the record without calling unpair

When unpair raises DeviceUnreachableError, the Hub answers 409 device_unreachable: "Device unreachable. Forget it instead? It might need a manual factory reset to pair again."

docs.title: fetch reads the whole device
docs.text:
async def fetch(self, device: TDevice) -> TDeviceState | None: ...

The Hub calls it right after pairing, on a manual refresh, and to revive a device that is unavailable. It is idempotent:

  • Read the whole device and return it: device with its full parameters list (ids from parameter_uuid, current values) and available. The Hub creates the parameters on the first fetch, then compares each one with what it stored: new and gone parameters, changed values. The Hub saves it. Report none of it as events: those are for changes the device starts itself.
  • Check its event subscription. Subscribe again only if it is gone. Never create a second one.
  • Finish in bounded time. Return None when the device doesn't answer, like a sleeping battery device: it is not a failure, and the Hub keeps what it has.

docs.title: Device → Hub
docs.text:
Use self.output (a ControllerOutput), injected by the Hub:

# New unpaired device found during discovery
await self.output.controller_did_receive_discovery(self, discovery)

# An already-discovered (unpaired) device changed its advertisement
await self.output.controller_did_update_discovery(self, discovery)

# A previously-discovered device is no longer visible
await self.output.controller_did_lose_discovery(self, discovery_id)

# Device connected; on start, report every paired device that answers.
# Never during pair_device: the Hub reports a new device itself once it saved it.
# Ids are keyword-only: pass physical_id= (device_id= is for relays passing on the Hub's id)
await self.output.controller_did_connect_device(self, physical_id=physical_id)

# A paired device became unreachable while the Hub is running
await self.output.controller_did_lose_device(self, physical_id=physical_id)

# Device reported new parameter values or events; the Hub saves their values
await self.output.controller_did_receive_events(self, events)

# A user-facing problem with the whole integration — a CTA, or (is_still_running=False) a failure
# that leaves it inactive. Plain language for the user; technical detail goes to the logs.
await self.output.controller_did_encounter_error(
    self, IntegrationError("server-unreachable", "The Acme server is unreachable — check that it is running")
)

# The problem is gone
await self.output.controller_did_resolve_error(self, "server-unreachable")

docs.title: last_error
docs.text:
Both Discovery and Device carry a last_error: str | None field. The integration owns this field entirely — the Hub only stores and exposes it.

Situation Action Connection attempt fails Set last_error to a human-readable message and call the appropriate output method (controller_did_receive_discovery, controller_did_update_discovery, etc.) Device fetch or command fails Set discovery.last_error / device.last_error accordingly Error is resolved Set last_error = None explicitly — the Hub never clears it automatically 
# On failure — surface the error to the user
discovery.last_error = "Connection timed out"
await self.output.controller_did_update_discovery(self, discovery)

# On recovery — clear it explicitly
discovery.last_error = None
await self.output.controller_did_update_discovery(self, discovery)

Device.last_error is persisted in the database, so stale errors survive restarts. Make sure to clear it whenever your integration successfully recovers, otherwise the error remains visible until explicitly resolved.

The natural places to clear it depend on the error kind — for connection errors, clear on successful connection or successful fetch; for discovery errors, clear when the device re-appears or its advertisement updates successfully. In general: wherever you can confirm the condition that caused the error no longer holds, that's where the None assignment belongs.

last_error is not limited to connection failures — use it for any condition worth surfacing to the user: authentication failures, unsupported firmware versions, misconfiguration, rate limiting, or any other integration-level problem. If the user should see it, put it here.

docs.title: controller_did_encounter_error
docs.text:
last_error is persistent per-device/discovery state — a flag on one device that stays until you clear it. controller_did_encounter_error is complementary: the way to report a controller-level problem that isn't tied to a single device. The problem stays active until you resolve it, or until the integration stops or restarts.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class IntegrationError:  # from majordom_integration_sdk import IntegrationError
    id: str
    message: str
    is_still_running: bool = True


async def controller_did_encounter_error(self, controller, error: IntegrationError) -> None: ...
async def controller_did_resolve_error(self, controller, error_id: str) -> None: ...
  • id — stable per condition, e.g. "server-unreachable" or "stick-unplugged": it links the report to its resolve. Reporting an active id again replaces it, so you can report on every failed attempt without piling up duplicates. Several ids can be active at once. Ids are scoped to your integration (the Hub and the app key an error by integration and id), and the hub- prefix is reserved for the errors the Hub reports on an integration's behalf.
  • message — plain language for the user, never a traceback. Put technical detail in the logs; put here only what the user should see, and fold any call-to-action right into the text.
  • is_still_running — False when the controller can no longer run. The Hub marks the integration inactive and tells the user it failed (and what to do, if actionable) — no technical dump. If the controller was running, the Hub then restarts it; when start() raises, it retries after 5, 30 and 120 seconds before it gives up. Keep the default True for a problem the integration keeps running through but the user should know about (a lost server it reconnects to, a user-fixable misconfiguration).

Call controller_did_resolve_error with the id once the condition no longer holds: the connection is back, the user fixed the setup. Resolving an id that isn't active does nothing, so you can resolve after every successful connection. The Hub keeps active errors in memory only (they are not saved) and drops all of an integration's errors when it stops or restarts, so a is_still_running=False error is gone once the Hub restarts the integration.

docs.title: Which one do I use?
docs.text:
There are five places an error can go. Pick by asking who it's for and how long it should stay:

Surface Use it for How long it lives Device.last_error / Discovery.last_error a problem with one device stays until you clear it controller_did_encounter_error the whole integration has a problem; is_still_running=False = it failed and stopped until resolved, or the integration restarts DeviceIdTakenError raised by check_device_id another record already holds the id this pairing would give; see Device ids returned to the app with this pairing attempt DeviceUnreachableError raised by unpair the device can't be reached to undo its pairing; see unpair returned to the app, which offers to forget the device MissingCredentialsError raised from pair_device the Hub lacks credentials (e.g. Wi-Fi) for one pairing; see Missing Hub credentials returned to the app with this pairing attempt any other error raised from pair_device this pairing failed; the Hub rolls it back and returns pairing_failed to the app. Don't also set last_error or report it with controller_did_encounter_error returned to the app with this pairing attempt logs (logger.*) technical detail, for you the developer log retention

What about a parameter failing? Parameters don't have an error field, on purpose. If one parameter fails (a rejected command, an unreadable value), tell the user at the device level and name the parameter in the message: device.last_error = "Brightness could not be set — the device rejected the command". Status codes and tracebacks go to the logs.

Two habits:

  • User surfaces get plain language — never a traceback or a protocol code.
  • One incident usually goes to two places: a detailed log line for you, plus one user-facing surface. Logs-only is fine only when the user can't see or fix anything.
# Recoverable, but the user must act; reported on every failed attempt, it stays one error:
await self.output.controller_did_encounter_error(
    self, IntegrationError("server-unreachable", "Matter server unreachable — check that it is running")
)

# ... and once connected again:
await self.output.controller_did_resolve_error(self, "server-unreachable")

# Fatal — the integration can't continue (the Hub restarts it, which clears the error):
await self.output.controller_did_encounter_error(
    self,
    IntegrationError("radio-lost", "The Zigbee coordinator is not responding and the integration has stopped.", False),
)

docs.title: The discoveries property
docs.text:
Return your current in-memory cache of unpaired, visible devices. The Hub polls this — do not trigger scanning here.

@property
def discoveries(self) -> dict[UUID, Discovery]:
    return self._discoveries  # maintained elsewhere, e.g. in a discovery event callback

The UUID for a given physical device must remain stable as long as it is visible.

docs.title: start_pairing_window(duration_sec, credentials=None)
docs.text:
async def start_pairing_window(self, duration_sec: int, credentials: ProvidedCredentials | None = None) -> None: ...

Optional. Override only if your protocol requires an explicit short-lived scan mode to surface new devices (e.g. Zigbee permit-join, BLE burst scan). Always-on discovery (mDNS, SSDP) does not need this. Default is a no-op.

credentials carries anything the user supplied when opening the window, before any device is discovered — e.g. a Z-Wave SmartStart QR code / DSK. It is None when the user gave none. The Hub relays it from POST start_pairing_window (target integration in the integration query parameter, credentials in the request body).

docs.title: What the Hub Gives
docs.text:
A controller is a Peripheral. It is constructed as Controller(platform, settings=None); keep these parameters when you override __init__. The runtime sets the rest before start().

Attribute Type Description self.platform Platform The host, frozen and shared by every peripheral: region, wifi, thread_dataset, documents_folder(self), device_repository(self) self.output ControllerOutput What it reports to the Hub; logs every call in library mode self.settings your Settings The validated settings; NoSettings when you declare none self.peripherals Peripherals What your needs are bound to, by family Call Returns self.peripherals.endpoint("zigbee") the Endpoint bound to that need; KeyError while it is unbound self.peripherals.endpoints("zigbee") every endpoint bound to an is_many need (e.g. several Zigbee sticks), as a list; empty while unbound self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER) the in-process peripheral bound to a typed need (BLE_ROUTER, ZEROCONF, UPNP_SSDP), typed by it; None while unbound

Device paths, server URLs, discovery and options all arrive here; see using a peripheral for a full example. Don't read them from environment variables or config files, and don't start your own mDNS, SSDP or Bluetooth stack. Read self.platform when you need a fact: a platform you kept holds the old ones.

docs.title: Needs and settings
docs.text:
needs is a class attribute: everything external the controller uses. Settings are a nested Settings model, named as the last type parameter.

from majordom_integration_sdk import Need

class ZigBeeController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter, "ZigBeeController.Settings"]):
    needs = [Need("zigbee", ZIGPY_DIALECTS)]  # ezsp, znp, deconz, xbee, zigate, ziggurat, blz, cc

    class Settings(BaseModel):
        channel: int = Field(15, ge=11, le=26, title="Channel")

    async def start(self):
        zigbee = self.peripherals.endpoint("zigbee")
        channel = self.settings.channel
        ...

HomeKit, which only uses the network, needs just ZEROCONF. Make a typed need optional with BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False). See Peripherals and Settings.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Each hook is optional and called while the controller runs. Return True when you handled the change in place; False has the runtime restart the controller. Several can fire at once: the controller restarts unless all return True. A hook that raises counts as False.

Hook Called when Default needed_peripheral_did_change(change) a bound need appeared, moved, or an optional one was lost; self.peripherals holds the new binding False settings_did_change(before) the user changed its settings; self.settings holds the new ones False platform_facts_did_change(before) region, Wi-Fi or Thread network changed; self.platform holds the new ones True

When a required need is lost, no hook is called: the runtime stops the controller and starts it again once the need is bound.

async def needed_peripheral_did_change(self, change: PeripheralChange) -> bool:
    if change.family == "thread":  # optional: Wi-Fi devices keep working without it
        self._border_router = change.after.url if change.after else None
        return True
    return False


async def settings_did_change(self, before: Settings) -> bool:
    if self.settings.channel != before.channel:
        return False  # start() forms the network on the channel: restart
    return True


async def platform_facts_did_change(self, before: Platform) -> bool:
    return self.platform.region == before.region  # start() sets the radio's region

docs.title: Staying connected
docs.text:
A service is recreated when its settings or bindings render it differently, and it may crash and come back. Nobody tells the controller. So don't let one connection live as long as the controller: keep a task that waits for the connection to drop and reconnects with backoff.

async def _stay_connected(self):
    """Reconnects whenever the server goes away, until stop() cancels it."""
    while True:
        await self._client.wait_closed()
        message = "Lost the connection to the Acme server, reconnecting."
        await self.output.controller_did_encounter_error(self, IntegrationError("server-unreachable", message))
        delay = self._RECONNECT_DELAY
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # 1, 2, 4, … 30, 30 seconds
            try:
                self._client = await self._connect()
                break
            except OSError as error:
                logger.info(f"The Acme server is not back yet: {error!r}")
                delay = min(delay * 2, self._RECONNECT_DELAY_MAX)
        await self.output.controller_did_resolve_error(self, "server-unreachable")

is_still_running=True (the default) tells the user the integration is degraded, not failed, until the error is resolved. Resolve it only once a connection held for STABLE_RUN seconds, so a server that answers and drops every time is still reported. While the connection is down, report the devices you reach through it as lost, and as connected again once it's back.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
class CredentialsType(str, Enum):
    code = "code"      # pin, e.g. 123-45-678 (HomeKit) or 1234-123-1234 (Matter)
    qr = "qr"          # raw QR data
    secret = "secret"  # e.g. AES key like in ESPHome
    button = "button"  # physical confirmation on the device; carries no value
    none = "none"      # pairing needs nothing from the user

    def with_mask(self, mask: str, hint: str | None = None) -> CredentialsOption: ...
    def with_hint(self, hint: str) -> CredentialsOption: ...

class CredentialsOption(Base):
    type: CredentialsType
    mask: str | None = None  # D = digit placeholder, other symbols unchanged: "DDD-DD-DDD" for "123-45-678"
    hint: str | None = None  # a short UI prompt, e.g. "Press the button on the device"

type CredentialsValue = str

class ProvidedCredentials(Base):
    type: CredentialsType
    value: CredentialsValue | None = None

class Discovery(Base):
    # technical
    id: UUID
    integration: NonEmptyStr
    expected_credentials_options: list[CredentialsOption]
    expiration: datetime | None = None
    # for UX
    transport: NonEmptyStr
    device_manufacturer: str | None
    device_name: NonEmptyStr
    device_category: str | None
    device_icon: str | None
    last_error: str | None = None  # set by the integration on failure, cleared (None) on recovery

    def accepts(self, credentials: ProvidedCredentials | None) -> bool: ...  # no credentials count as `none`

A discovery advertises every way it can actually be paired — expected_credentials_options — since a device can support more than one simultaneously (e.g. a Matter device with both a QR code and a manual pairing code). List every option the device supports, in the order you'd like the app to prefer them. with_mask() and with_hint() are the short form of CredentialsOption(type=..., mask=..., hint=...); a bare type is an option without mask or hint:

Discovery(
    ...,
    expected_credentials_options=[
        CredentialsType.code.with_mask("DDD-DD-DDD", hint="On the box"),
        CredentialsType.button.with_hint("Press the button on the device"),
        CredentialsType.qr,
    ],
)
# on the wire: [{"type": "code", "mask": "DDD-DD-DDD", "hint": "On the box"}, {"type": "button", ...}, ...]
Type The user... ProvidedCredentials.value code types a setup code, formatted by mask the code qr scans a setup QR code the raw QR payload secret enters a key (e.g. an ESPHome API encryption key) the key button physically confirms on the device (Improv, a setup button) none: a confirmation step none does nothing; pairing needs no input none

For example, ESPHome offers both none and secret for a node the Hub already gave a key to earlier: none pairs with the key the Hub kept, secret covers a node reflashed with its own key.

Pairing requests then send back ProvidedCredentials, pairing the actual value with which type it is, instead of a bare string. Your pair_device() must validate the supplied type against the discovery's options before using it — discovery.accepts(credentials) does it. Don't trust discovery.credentials from whatever your own discovery-time heuristic guessed; validate against what the caller explicitly asserts.

docs.title: Missing Hub credentials
docs.text:
When the Hub itself lacks something a pairing needs (a Hub on Ethernet has no Wi-Fi to give a node set up over BLE), raise MissingCredentialsError(type) from pair_device before touching the device. No record is created and the Hub returns the error to the app, which asks the user for the credentials and retries (see POST /device in the Hub API reference).

from majordom_integration_sdk.errors import MissingCredentialsError

error = MissingCredentialsError(MissingCredentialsError.WIFI)  # "wifi" is the default
str(error)                                                     # "Missing credentials: wifi"

type is a lower_snake_case string, so an integration can add its own and documents it; the app maps it to the screen to show.

type The Hub lacks... wifi a Wi-Fi network (SSID and password) to give a device thread a Thread network (dataset) to give a device

ESPHome raises wifi for a BLE (Improv) discovery when the Hub has no Wi-Fi to give.

docs.text:
class ParameterDataType(StrEnum):
    none = "none"        # e.g. button
    bool = "bool"
    integer = "integer"
    decimal = "decimal"  # python float
    enum = "enum"        # integer with string representation
    string = "string"
    struct = "struct"    # multi-field object (e.g. command arguments); see "Commands with arguments"
    data = "data"        # binary data, base64 encoded at high level

class ParameterUnit(StrEnum):
    plain = "plain"
    percentage = "percentage"
    second = "second"
    hertz = "hertz"
    kilogram = "kilogram"
    arcdegree = "arcdegree"
    meters = "meters"
    mps = "mps"      # meters per second
    mps2 = "mps2"    # meters per second squared
    rpm = "rpm"
    newton = "newton"
    joule = "joule"
    watt = "watt"
    celsius = "celsius"
    kelvin = "kelvin"
    volt = "volt"
    ampere = "ampere"
    lux = "lux"
    pascal = "pascal"
    ppm = "ppm"      # parts per million, air quality
    bytes = "bytes"
    bps = "bps"      # bytes per second

class ParameterRole(StrEnum):
    sensor = 'sensor'   # read-only
    control = 'control' # read-write
    event = 'event'     # fire-and-forget


class ParameterVisibility(StrEnum):
    user = "user"  # main, everyday interaction, device screen widgets (on/off, brightness, volume)
    setting = "setting"  # user-configurable but behind am extra "settings"/"advanced" tap: configured once and rarely touched again; or diagnostic readings (RSSI, firmware version)
    system = "system"  # hidden under-the-hood wirings; not visible to the user

# Generic over its value type V — value, valid_values keys, and default_value all share V
# (an int parameter has int labels and an int default; a str parameter is str throughout).
class Parameter[V](UUIdentifable):
    id: UUID
    name: str
    description: str | None = None   # manufacturer-provided, read-only
    note: str | None = None          # user-editable, MajorDom-side only
    data_type: ParameterDataType
    unit: ParameterUnit = ParameterUnit.plain
    role: ParameterRole
    visibility: ParameterVisibility
    min_value: int | float | None = None
    max_value: int | float | None = None
    min_step: int | float | None = None       # smallest increment for a numeric parameter
    valid_values: dict[V, str] | None = None  # allowed values → labels; for enums (numbers: use min/max/step)
    fields: list["Parameter"] | None = None   # sub-parameters for data_type=struct (e.g. command args)
    default_value: set[V] | V | None = None   # main-parameter tap value(s): one = button, a set = cycle
    integration_data: Any                     # protocol-specific payload, opaque to the Hub

    @property
    def can_be_main_parameter(self) -> bool:
        return self.visibility == ParameterVisibility.user and bool(
            self.data_type in (ParameterDataType.bool, ParameterDataType.none)
            or self.default_value is not None
            or self.valid_values
        )

class ParameterState[V](Parameter[V]):
    value: V | None = None   # pythonic value (int/bool/str/float/dict/...), not bytes

docs.title: main_parameter and default_value
docs.text:
Device.main_parameter points at the one Parameter behind the room-tile tap (a toggle in most cases — e.g. OnOff for a light, not Brightness). A parameter is eligible (can_be_main_parameter) when it's user-visible and a tap does something meaningful: a bool or none command inherently, an enum through its valid_values, or — for any data type — a default_value.

default_value is what makes an arbitrary parameter tappable (any data type) and curates what a tap sends — set it to one value for a button, or a set for a cycle (e.g. brightness {0, 80} so a dimmer taps like an on/off switch). It shares the parameter's value type V. (valid_values only describes a parameter's allowed values and their labels — it doesn't carry the tap value.)

See Parameter UX for how each case behaves on tap and how to pick the main parameter and good visibility.

docs.title: Commands with arguments
docs.text: Some integrations (e.g. Matter) expose commands that take a list of arguments — for those, the command itself is modeled as a Parameter and each of its arguments as a nested Parameter in fields: command = parameter, argument = sub-parameter. This is a convention on top of the generic schema, not a separate concept. If your integration's commands don't take structured arguments, you leave fields unset.

docs.title: Example Integration
docs.text:
This page is a narrative walkthrough of the example controller that ships in the integration-template repository. The template is the source of truth for the actual, CI-verified code — start there with Use this template, then read this page to understand why each piece looks the way it does.

The example isn't real protocol code — there's no such thing as "AcmeProtocol" or "AcmeClient". Every piece that would normally come from a real device library is marked # pseudo so you know it's made up. Everything else — module layout, method names, signatures, how the pieces call into each other — matches the real SDK interfaces described in Implementing a Controller, Storing Data, and Data Models Reference. Read this page alongside those, not instead of them.

If this is your first integration, don't worry about understanding every line the first time through. Scaffold from the template, rename Acme to your protocol, and start replacing the # pseudo bits with calls into your actual device library one at a time.

More examples

This page is a pedagogical walkthrough. For real, production integrations to learn from — HomeKit, Zigbee, Matter, and more — browse the official MajorDom integrations at github.com/orgs/MajorDom-Systems/repositories?q=integration-.

docs.title: The controller at a glance
docs.text:
Before the details, here's the whole shape of a finished controller — every method you implement, in one place. Bodies are elided (...); the sections group them by direction of data flow. If you're new to OOP or SDKs, read this as the "table of contents" for the rest of the page.

class MyController(AbstractController[MyDevice, MyParameter]):
    name = "My Protocol"  # optional — auto-derived from the class name otherwise

    # ── Lifecycle ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    async def start(self) -> None: ...   # connect, start discovery, restore already-paired devices
    async def stop(self)  -> None: ...   # cancel tasks, stop discovery, close connections

    # ── Discovery  (Device → Hub) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    @property
    def discoveries(self) -> dict[UUID, Discovery]: ...   # cached snapshot of unpaired devices
    #   when a device appears, call:
    #     await self.output.controller_did_receive_discovery(self, discovery)

    # ── Pairing ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    async def start_pairing_window(self, duration_sec: int, credentials=None) -> None: ...  # optional (e.g. Zigbee)
    async def pair_device(self, discovery, draft, credentials) -> DeviceState: ...  # fill the draft: commission, identity only
    async def unpair(self, device: MyDevice) -> None: ...                  # also the rollback of a failed pairing

    # ── Control & read  (Hub → Device) ───────────────────────────────────────
    async def send_command(self, command, device, parameter) -> None: ...  # set a value / run command
    async def fetch(self, device: MyDevice) -> DeviceState | None: ...      # read the whole device + re-subscribe
    async def identify(self, device: MyDevice) -> None: ...                 # blink / beep the device

    # ── Events  (Device → Hub) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    #   on an incoming device update, call:
    #     await self.output.controller_did_receive_events(self, [DeviceParameterChange(...)])

docs.title: Module Layout
docs.text:
Your integration is a standalone package (majordom_<protocol>/), scaffolded from the template:

majordom_acme/
├── __init__.py        # exports peripherals(platform): [AcmeController(platform)]
├── controller.py      # AbstractController subclass — the only file the Hub actually calls into
├── models.py          # typed integration_data schemas — what MajorDom persists to disk for you
└── mapper.py          # protocol <-> MajorDom conversions — pure functions, no I/O

docs.title: models.py — typed integration_data
docs.text:
integration_data is a free-form field MajorDom lets every integration attach to its own Device/Parameter records, for protocol-specific bookkeeping (an auth token, an internal id, etc.). Subclass the SDK schemas to give it a typed shape — the Hub then (de)serializes it for you. Here we remember the device's network hostname (not IP — see the discovery note below) and an auth token the Acme protocol handed us during pairing:

from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.base import Base
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.device import Device, DeviceState
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.parameter import Parameter, ParameterState

class AcmeDeviceIntegrationData(Base):
    device_hostname: str          # a hostname, resolved to the current IP by the OS
    auth_token: str | None = None

class AcmeParameterIntegrationData(Base):
    acme_property_name: str       # the name Acme's own API uses for this property

# Device/DeviceState and Parameter/ParameterState are pairs: the "State" version carries the
# same fields plus the actual live value(s). You need both — see Storing Data for why.
class AcmeDevice(Device):
    integration_data: AcmeDeviceIntegrationData

class AcmeDeviceState(DeviceState):
    integration_data: AcmeDeviceIntegrationData

class AcmeParameter(Parameter):
    integration_data: AcmeParameterIntegrationData

class AcmeParameterState(ParameterState):
    integration_data: AcmeParameterIntegrationData

To make the Hub hand you these subclasses (with integration_data already parsed), the controller overrides device_type/parameter_type — see Storing Data.

docs.title: mapper.py — pure conversions
docs.text:
Keep protocol↔domain conversions here: pure functions that turn "whatever your device library gives you" into MajorDom's Parameter/Device types. No I/O, no self.platform, nothing that touches the network or database — so you (or a test) can call them directly without a real device. A property's kind maps to a ParameterDataType; whether it's writable maps to ParameterRole.control vs ParameterRole.sensor:

from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.parameter import ParameterDataType, ParameterRole, ParameterVisibility
from .models import AcmeParameter, AcmeParameterIntegrationData

class AcmeMapper:
    def parameter_from_acme_property(self, parameter_id, acme_property: dict) -> AcmeParameter:
        data_type = ParameterDataType.bool if acme_property["kind"] == "bool" else ParameterDataType.integer
        role = ParameterRole.control if acme_property["writable"] else ParameterRole.sensor
        return AcmeParameter(
            id=parameter_id,
            name=acme_property["name"],
            data_type=data_type,
            role=role,
            visibility=ParameterVisibility.user,   # show on the device's main screen; see Data Models for setting/system
            integration_data=AcmeParameterIntegrationData(acme_property_name=acme_property["name"]),
        )

device_uuid/parameter_uuid are helpers on AbstractController (Helper Methods) — call them from the controller and pass the resulting ids into the mapper, since the mapper has no access to self.

docs.title: controller.py — the walkthrough
docs.text:
The package's peripherals(platform) builds the controller. It declares its identity as a class attribute and subclasses the generic AbstractController:

from majordom_integration_sdk import DeviceUnreachableError
from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import ZEROCONF
from majordom_integration_sdk.controller import AbstractController
from .models import AcmeDevice, AcmeParameter

class AcmeController(AbstractController[AcmeDevice, AcmeParameter]):
    name = "Acme"                 # shown to the user; its slug "acme" is the key
    needs = [ZEROCONF]  # Acme devices announce themselves over mDNS
    _mapper = AcmeMapper()        # stateless, so one shared instance is fine

docs.title: Lifecycle: start / stop
docs.text:
start() runs once its needs are bound (at boot, when enabled, after a restart); stop() on shutdown or before a restart. Two things happen in start(): register for discovery (keep the returned cancel closure for stop), and — crucially — reconnect to already-paired devices. On every Hub restart, start() is your only chance to do that; skip it and paired devices look "stuck" until re-paired. controller_did_connect_device isn't just for "just finished pairing" — call it any time a device becomes reachable, including here at boot, to flip device.available back to True:

async def start(self):
    self._discoveries = {}
    self._subscriptions = {}  # physical id -> cancel closure
    self._client = AcmeClient()  # pseudo
    self._cancel_discovery = self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF).register(self, {"_acme._tcp.local."})

    async with self.platform.device_repository(self) as repo:
        for device in await repo.get_all(as_=AcmeDevice):  # scoped to this integration's key
            self._subscribe(device)
            await self.output.controller_did_connect_device(self, physical_id=device.physical_id)

async def stop(self):
    self._cancel_discovery()
    await self._client.close()  # pseudo

docs.title: Discovery callbacks: identify by hostname, never by IP
docs.text:
Zeroconf (self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF)) calls three listener methods (zeroconf_did_discover_service, ..._update_service, ..._remove_service) because you passed self to register(). Derive the stable discovery id from info.name (the mDNS instance name), which stays constant across discover/update/remove for the same physical device — not from its IP address:

If you keyed the id off the IP, a routine DHCP lease renewal would change the address and the Hub would think a brand-new device appeared instead of recognizing the one it already knew. Storing a hostname in integration_data (rather than an IP) sidesteps this entirely: the OS resolves the hostname to the current IP for you, so a paired device changing IP requires no work at all. If you must store an IP, you'd have to update it and re-verify reachability on every update event.

_update_service only reports a device still in your discoveries dict (an unpaired device whose advertisement changed); _remove_service gives you only name, so pop by the same derived id and call controller_did_lose_discovery.

docs.title: pair_device: fill the draft
docs.text:
The Hub builds a draft from what the user entered (name, room, icon) and hands it to you with the discovery. You fill it in and return it. The Hub saves it, so you don't touch the repository and you report nothing about the device yet.

Always validate that the credentials actually sent match the discovery's advertised options — never trust your own discovery-time guess:

async def pair_device(
    self, discovery: Discovery, draft: DeviceState, credentials: ProvidedCredentials | None
) -> DeviceState:
    if not credentials or credentials.type not in discovery.expected_credentials_options:
        raise ValueError("Unsupported or missing credentials for this discovery")

    serial = await self._client.read_serial(discovery.id)  # pseudo, read-only
    draft.physical_id = self.device_uuid(serial)  # your lookup id; draft.id is the Hub's, never change it
    await self.check_device_id(draft.physical_id, draft)  # raises DeviceIdTakenError: nothing irreversible ran yet
    ...

The device now has its physical_id, distinct from its (temporary) discovery id. Build it from the serial number, a string unique to that device. A name or an address two devices share would give them the same id. check_device_id raises DeviceIdTakenError when another record already holds the id, so the user gets a clear refusal and the device is left untouched.

Now the irreversible step. Write what it changes to integration_data first, then run it. If anything fails, the Hub calls unpair(draft), which reads the draft to know what to undo. Pairing must also be idempotent: a retry may find the device as an earlier attempt left it, so reuse a key the draft already carries instead of refusing:

    known = draft.integration_data.session_key if draft.integration_data else None  # pseudo: pairing onto a record
    key = known or new_session_key()  # pseudo
    draft.integration_data = AcmeDeviceIntegrationData(device_hostname=hostname, session_key=key)
    await self._client.pair(discovery.id, code=credentials.value, session_key=key)  # pseudo, irreversible; a no-op when already paired with this key

    draft.available = True
    return draft

Don't map parameters, call _subscribe or controller_did_connect_device here. The Hub saves the draft, reports the device connected, and then calls fetch, which reads the parameters and subscribes.

docs.title: unpair: also the rollback
docs.text:
unpair tells the device to forget the pairing (the Hub removes its own record). It is also what the Hub calls to roll back a failed pairing, or one it failed to save, with the draft as you left it. So it must cope with a draft at any stage (no integration_data, a device already reset), undo everything pairing did in reverse order, never wait for the user, and be safe to call again. It talks to the device only: when the device can't be reached, raise DeviceUnreachableError and change nothing else. The app then offers the user to forget the device, which only the Hub does.

async def unpair(self, device: AcmeDevice):
    data = device.integration_data
    if data is None:  # pair_device failed before the irreversible step: nothing to undo
        return
    self._unsubscribe(device)  # stop listening; a no-op when not subscribed
    try:
        await self._client.forget(data.device_hostname, session_key=data.session_key)  # pseudo; a no-op when already forgotten
    except AcmeError as error:  # pseudo: the device is gone
        raise DeviceUnreachableError(f"{device.physical_id} is unreachable") from error

docs.title: identify / fetch
docs.text:
Thin wrappers over your client: identify makes the device blink/beep so the user can find it.

fetch reads the whole device, and it is safe to call any number of times. It reads every parameter with its current value and returns the device with them: the Hub saves them and tells the app what changed. It checks the subscription and subscribes again only if it is gone, never twice. A sleeping battery device that doesn't answer returns None: not a failure.

async def fetch(self, device: AcmeDevice) -> AcmeDeviceState | None:
    try:
        properties = await asyncio.wait_for(self._client.get_properties(device.integration_data.device_hostname), 10)  # pseudo
    except TimeoutError:
        return None
    if device.physical_id not in self._subscriptions:
        self._subscribe(device)
    parameters = self._mapper.parameters(self, device.physical_id, properties)  # pseudo: with their current values
    return AcmeDeviceState(**device.model_dump(), parameters=parameters, available=True)

docs.title: send_command: Hub → device
docs.text:
Called when the user changes something in the app. command.value is the new value; parameter tells you which property — look up the protocol's own name from your integration_data:

async def send_command(self, command: DeviceCommand, device: AcmeDevice, parameter: AcmeParameter):
    await self._client.set_property(
        device.integration_data.device_hostname,
        parameter.integration_data.acme_property_name,
        command.value,
    )  # pseudo

docs.title: _subscribe: device → Hub
docs.text:
Called once per device — from fetch after pairing and once per already-paired device at boot. Whenever the device's own state changes, report it. Because protocol callbacks are usually plain (non-async), you schedule the async report as a task:

from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.event import DeviceParameterChange

def _subscribe(self, device: AcmeDevice):
    def on_property_changed(acme_property_name: str, value):
        event = DeviceParameterChange(
            physical_id=device.physical_id,
            parameter_id=self.parameter_uuid(device.physical_id, acme_property_name),
            value=value,
        )
        asyncio.create_task(self.output.controller_did_receive_events(self, [event]))

    def on_availability_changed(is_available: bool):
        # Optional mid-session availability: report only if your protocol can detect a *paired*
        # device dropping/returning while the Hub runs. If it can't, omit this entirely.
        cb = (self.output.controller_did_connect_device if is_available
              else self.output.controller_did_lose_device)
        asyncio.create_task(cb(self, physical_id=device.physical_id))

    self._subscriptions[device.physical_id] = self._client.subscribe(
        device.integration_data.device_hostname,
        on_property_changed=on_property_changed,
        on_availability_changed=on_availability_changed,
    )  # pseudo: returns a cancel closure; `_unsubscribe` pops it and calls it

docs.title: What's Deliberately Left Out
docs.text:
The example skips a few things your real integration will likely need, so it doesn't obscure the shape of the interface itself:

  • Error handling — set discovery.last_error / device.last_error on failures (see Implementing a Controller: last_error).
  • start_pairing_window — only implement it if your protocol needs an explicit, short-lived scan mode (Zigbee permit-join, BLE burst scan). Always-on discovery (mDNS, SSDP) doesn't need it.
  • Retry/backoff, connection pooling, rate limiting — whatever your protocol's client needs; the SDK prescribes nothing here.
  • Implementing the protocol yourself — the example assumes AcmeClient already exists as a high-level SDK (pair, get_properties, set_property, ...). Real protocols don't always have one; if yours doesn't, you may implement the transport, connection management, and serialization directly inside your integration. That's expected. The framework (AbstractController, the discovery peripherals, the Device/Parameter models) is deliberately independent of any protocol's implementation details — and, the discovery providers and data models in particular being plain public SDK, can be reused standalone (e.g. to build a protocol library outside MajorDom entirely).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Test your controller against simulated devices with the SDK's majordom_integration_sdk.testing doubles — build_test_platform() plus RecordingControllerOutput, and FakeZeroconf for the ZEROCONF need — rather than real hardware. See Testing and the template's own tests/ for the pattern.

docs.title: Parameter UX
docs.text:
Every parameter your controller exposes ends up somewhere in the MajorDom apps. This page shows you how to decide where each one goes and how it behaves — so a device feels polished instead of showing a wall of raw protocol fields.

In most cases the protocol alone can't make these calls for you. Whether a field is an everyday control, a rare setting, or an internal constant is usually something you decide, per parameter. The recipe below makes those decisions easy.

The fields themselves (visibility, main_parameter, default_value, bounds) are defined in Data Models; this page is about choosing good values for them.

docs.title: The four buckets
docs.text:
Two fields control placement: Device.main_parameter (one UUID) and Parameter.visibility (user / setting / system).

Bucket Where the user sees it main The one-tap action on the room tile — usually a toggle. Set device.main_parameter. user The device screen (tap the device) — everyday controls and live readings. visibility = user settings Behind a "Settings" tap — set once, rarely touched. visibility = setting system Hidden — internal wiring. visibility = system

Goal: keep the user list short. A light should show on/off, brightness, color — not 20 diagnostic fields. A device with 20+ user parameters is usually over-exposed — most of them probably belong in settings or system. (A custom DIY device with genuinely many controls is the rare exception.)

docs.title: How to pick a bucket
docs.text:
First, decide whether it is a parameter at all:

  • Never used → skip it.
  • Used only by the integration (encryption keys, tokens, caches) → integration_data, not a parameter.
  • Needed only to pair (a pairing PIN such as 123-45-678) → it reaches the integration once, as the pairing credentials (ProvidedCredentials). Never store it.

Then pick its visibility — take the first rule that matches:

  1. Not for the UI, but MajorDom may use it (in automations, via the API, programmatically, or in the UI in dev mode): infrastructure (pairing machinery, firmware update, group management), a secret MajorDom needs, metadata about another parameter (a device-reported min/max limit, a scaling factor, a capability flag) → system. For metadata, keep its value: use it as the real parameter's bounds (see Where bounds come from).
  2. Something people change every day? (on/off, brightness, target temperature, fan mode) → user
  3. A live reading people look at? (temperature, lock state, battery %) → user
  4. Something people configure once or rarely, or a diagnostic reading? (report interval, transition time, calibration, state on powering on, user-set ranges and limits; RSSI, uptime, firmware version) → setting
  5. Everything else → system

A keypad PIN (a code the user types to operate a lock or alarm panel) is not a secret to hide: make it an argument of the command it unlocks, optionally with a default-code setting.

One habit worth copying from the built-in integrations: when in doubt, hide it. Default unknown parameters to system and promote to user only the ones you've deliberately chosen. That way a new or odd parameter quietly stays hidden instead of cluttering the screen.

docs.title: The one-tap main parameter
docs.text:
Device.main_parameter is the device's quick action — the single control invoked when the user taps the device's tile on the home screen or a widget without opening the device (its full parameter list), and what a programmatic "tap" triggers without having to fetch state and pick a parameter. Set it and the device gets a one-tap action from anywhere; leave it unset and the user has to open the device and choose a parameter to do anything.

Parameter.can_be_main_parameter tells you which parameters qualify. A candidate must have user visibility — the main action is the most exposed control of all, so a settings or system parameter can never be it. Beyond that, the tap behaves differently depending on the parameter:

Main parameter Tap behaviour bool toggle — flips between on and off none (an argument-less command like Toggle) button — fires the command enum (has valid_values) cycle — each tap advances through its values, wrapping around default_value = one value button — every tap sends that same value default_value = two values toggle — alternates between the two default_value = three or more values cycle — advances through them, wrapping around

So a main parameter isn't limited to "do the same thing every time": a bool toggles, an enum steps through its states — and by setting default_value you can give any parameter a one-tap action. The number of values decides the behaviour — one = a button, two = a toggle, three or more = a cycle. Most of the time it's a two-value toggle (0 and some preferred value — e.g. brightness {0, 80} so a dimmer tile taps like an on/off switch). The same mechanism narrows an enum's cycle to a subset (just {off, on} for a fan) — set default_value to one value or a set; labels for the values come from valid_values. You don't compute any of this in your integration: when a tap produces a value-less command, the Hub derives the value to send (from the stored state, via Parameter.main_cycle + next_main_parameter_value) and hands your send_command a concrete value. Only a none-type command arrives value-less — you just fire it. If the device reports a value that isn't in the cycle, the next tap sends the first one, so it always recovers to a sane state.

More on main_parameter and default_value at the model level: Data Models.

docs.title: Where bounds come from
docs.text:
A parameter's min_value / max_value / unit should come from the best source available, in this order:

  1. The device itself — many devices expose their own limit attributes (e.g. MinLevel / MaxLevel). Read those at runtime; they're the truth for this device.
  2. Your spec tables — values you wrote down from the protocol spec.
  3. The wire type — e.g. a uint8 is 0–255. Last resort.

The limit attributes in step 1 are the same ones rule 3 sent to system — hidden from the UI, but their values still power the real parameter's bounds. If a unit or range you'd expect is missing everywhere, log a warning: that's how you notice a quirky device.

docs.title: Users can override you
docs.text: Treat your mapping as a good default, not the final word. Parameter.visibility is patchable by the user (ParameterVisibilityPatch), and metadata should stay tunable too. Devices lie and people have preferences — curate the best out-of-the-box experience, and let users adjust it.

docs.title: Check your work
docs.text:
The SDK ships advisory warnings you can run after building a device's parameters (majordom_integration_sdk.parameter_audit). They flag:

  • too many user parameters on one device (over-exposure),
  • two user parameters with nearly the same name (one is probably redundant),
  • missing expected metadata (unit/range) — a quirky-device signal.

They warn, never fail — many genuine controls can be fine; the warning just says "look at this."

If your protocol library lets you enumerate every possible parameter (zigpy and Matter's chip both do), you can go further and audit the whole protocol at once — the Zigbee and Matter integrations each ship scripts/param_ux_audit.py for that, wired into CI. For a small or cloud-based protocol, just map your real test devices and eyeball the four buckets per device.

See also: Data Models, Implementing a Controller.

docs.title: Peripherals
docs.text:
An integration never opens /dev/ttyUSB0, starts its own Bluetooth scanner, or reads a server URL from an environment variable. It declares what it needs, and the Hub hands it over in self.peripherals once something can serve it. The same code then works with any supported stick, a multi-PAN radio, or a server running elsewhere.

Everything around an integration is a peripheral: a radio, a Bluetooth router, a Docker service, even your controller. Each one needs capabilities and provides them. A capability is a family/dialect pair: the family says what it is (zigbee), the dialect how to talk to it (ezsp).

docs.title: In-process capabilities
docs.text:
Objects you call directly. Need them by the SDK's typed needs, from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities.

Need Capability What you get Docs BLE_ROUTER ble/router a BLERouter: discovery, connections and leases over every Bluetooth radio Bluetooth LE ZEROCONF mdns/zeroconf a Zeroconf browser (mDNS / DNS-SD) Zeroconf UPNP_SSDP upnp/ssdp an SSDP listener SSDP

docs.title: Radios
docs.text:
USB sticks the Hub recognises, and radios soldered on the Hub's board. You get a serial path (/dev/serial/by-id/…) and its serial settings in params (baud, flow_control).

Capability Radio zigbee/ezsp Silicon Labs stick with Zigbee firmware thread/spinel Silicon Labs stick with Thread (RCP) firmware multipan/silabs-cpc Silicon Labs stick with multi-PAN firmware zwave/serial-api any Z-Wave stick

Other sticks are recognised by the UsbDrivers integrations bring (see Recognising a stick).

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Docker services the SDK runs while something needs them.

Service Needs Provides otbr (OpenThread Border Router) thread/spinel thread/otbr-rest: a Thread border router's REST API, shared silabs-multiprotocol multipan/silabs-cpc zigbee/ezsp over TCP and thread/otbr-rest, from one multi-PAN stick

Integrations bring their own services the same way, see Bringing a Docker service.

docs.title: Host and raw Bluetooth
docs.text:
