Capability What it is ip the Hub's network, shared by everyone ble/bluez, ble/silabs-cpc-hci, ble/esphome-proxy raw Bluetooth radios: taken by the router only. Use BLE_ROUTER

Facts about the Hub (radio region, Wi-Fi network, Thread network) aren't peripherals: read them from self.platform, see Settings.

See all peripherals and how they connect →

docs.title: TL;DR: using a peripheral
docs.text:
Declare needs, then read what they are bound to in start():

from majordom_integration_sdk import AbstractController, Device, Need, Parameter
from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLE_ROUTER


class AcmeController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    needs = [
        Need("zigbee", ["ezsp", "znp"]),  # every dialect your library speaks
        BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False),  # optional: works without it
    ]

    async def start(self):
        radio = self.peripherals.endpoint("zigbee")
        self._client = await connect_radio(radio.dialect, radio.url, baud=radio.params.get("baud"))

        if router := self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER):  # None while unbound
            self._cancel_ble = router.register(self, MATCHERS)
Read Returns self.peripherals.endpoint(family) the Endpoint bound to that need: url, dialect, params self.peripherals.endpoints(family) every endpoint of an is_many need, as a list self.peripherals.instance(NEED) the object of a typed need (BLE_ROUTER, ZEROCONF, UPNP_SSDP), or None

Connect to the url you're given and never build one yourself: it may point at a stick, a TCP socket, or a server somewhere else.

docs.title: TL;DR: bringing a Docker service
docs.text:
When your protocol runs behind a server, ship the server with the integration as a Service. The Hub runs it in Docker while your controller runs. Z-Wave is the simple case: zwave-js-server opens the stick, and the controller talks to its WebSocket API.

from majordom_integration_sdk import AbstractController, Device, Endpoint, Need, Parameter, Peripheral, Platform, Service


def zwave_js_server() -> Service:
    return Service(
        "zwave-js-server",
        needs=[Need("zwave", ["serial-api"])],  # the stick
        provides=[Endpoint("zwave", "zwave-js-ws", "ws://127.0.0.1:{ports.api}")],
        ports={"api": 3000},  # preferred: the Hub picks another one when it's taken
        compose={
            "image": "ghcr.io/kpine/zwave-js-server@sha256:…",  # pin by digest
            "network_mode": "host",
            "command": ["server", "/dev/zwave", "--host", "{host.listen_address}", "--port", "{ports.api}"],
            "devices": ["{peripherals.zwave.url}:/dev/zwave"],
            "volumes": ["{data}:/cache"],
            "environment": {"RF_REGION": "{platform.region}"},
        },
    )


class ZwaveController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    needs = [Need("zwave", ["zwave-js-ws"])]  # what the service provides

    async def start(self):
        url = self.peripherals.endpoint("zwave").url  # ws://127.0.0.1:3000
        ...


def peripherals(platform: Platform) -> list[Peripheral]:
    """The integration's entry point: the Hub runs everything it returns."""
    return [zwave_js_server(), ZwaveController(platform)]

That's all: the Hub finds the stick, starts the container with the stick's path, waits until its port answers, and starts the controller with the server's URL. Build a new Service on every peripherals() call.

compose is a Docker Compose service (typed as ComposeService). Its strings are templates:

Template Becomes {peripherals.<family>.url} the URL bound to one of the service's needs, e.g. the stick's path; empty while an optional need is unbound {peripherals.<family>.params[<name>]} a parameter of that endpoint, e.g. baud {ports.<name>} the host port the Hub picked for that port {data} the service's own data folder; mount it to keep state {settings.<field>} a field of the service's settings {platform.<fact>} a Hub fact, e.g. {platform.region} {host.listen_address} where a host-network service listens: loopback by default. Listen there, never on 0.0.0.0 {host.interface}, {host.uid}, {host.gid} the Hub's network interface; its user and group, for a container that writes its data as the Hub

A format spec renders text by the value: {x:?text} renders text when x isn't empty, {x:!text} when it is. A list item that renders empty is left out, so "volumes": ["{peripherals.ble.url:?/run/dbus:/run/dbus:ro}"] mounts the system bus only while an adapter is bound. Write {{ and }} for literal braces.

The params of the endpoints a service provides are templates too: that's how it tells its consumer what it got, e.g. params={"adapter": "{peripherals.ble.url}"}.

The service may be recreated or crash at any time. Keep the controller reconnecting.

docs.title: Needs
docs.text:
Need(family, dialects=(), is_required=True, is_many=False)
  • Dialects: list every one your client speaks. With none, any dialect of the family is accepted: only for what the host shares, like Need("ip").
  • Required (the default): the controller starts once the need is bound, and stops while it's lost. Meanwhile the app shows the integration as waiting for it.
  • Optional (is_required=False): the controller runs without it, and gets it once something can serve it. For a typed need: BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False).
  • Many (is_many=True): every matching endpoint, as a list.

An endpoint is exclusive by default, as a serial port opens once: the first consumer takes it. A shared one (is_shared=True), like a border router or ip, serves everyone.

docs.title: When a peripheral comes or goes
docs.text: What happens The controller A required need is lost (stick unplugged, server gone) is stopped, and started again once it's back A need appears or moves, an optional one is lost gets needed_peripheral_did_change(); restarted unless it returns True Its settings or the Hub's facts change gets settings_did_change() or platform_facts_did_change(), the same way A service it uses restarts isn't told: it reconnects itself

docs.title: Bringing peripherals along
docs.text: A controller's provides may hold peripherals too: they run while it does. When the list changes, tell the Hub with await self.output.controller_did_change_provided(self). The common case is a Bluetooth proxy: a device with its own Bluetooth radio, lent to the router as a BLEProxy. See Adding a BLE proxy.

docs.title: Recognising a stick: UsbDriver
docs.text:
The Hub recognises Silicon Labs and Z-Wave sticks itself. If your integration talks to a stick directly and it's of another kind, export a UsbDriver from peripherals(): identify(path) returns the firmware the stick runs (or None when it isn't yours), and firmwares says what each firmware provides, {device} being the stick's path.

from majordom_integration_sdk import Endpoint, UsbDriver


class AcmeDriver(UsbDriver):
    name = "acme"
    firmwares = {"acme-zigbee": [Endpoint("zigbee", "acme", "{device}", params={"baud": 115200})]}

    async def identify(self, path: str) -> str | None:
        return "acme-zigbee" if await probe_acme(path) else None

The Hub asks each driver once per stick.

docs.title: Dependency trees
docs.text: The Hub resolves a whole chain of needs on its own: a controller needs a service, the service needs a radio or another service. A few more complex cases, as examples.

docs.title: Matter: a service, an optional border router, Bluetooth
docs.text:
MatterController            needs matter/matter-server, ble/router (optional)
├── matterjs-server         the integration's own Service: needs ip, thread/otbr-rest (optional)
│   └── otbr                the SDK's Service: needs thread/spinel
│       └── a Thread stick
│     (or silabs-multiprotocol, on a multi-PAN stick)
└── the Bluetooth router    lent to matterjs-server for commissioning

matterjs-server needs only ip, so Matter runs on any Hub. Its optional Thread need makes the Hub start a border router whenever a stick can serve one; nothing in the integration says which. The border router tells the Hub the Thread network it formed, and the controller reads it as self.platform.thread_dataset. Commissioning over Bluetooth holds a lease for the whole flow.

docs.title: Zigbee: one need, many sticks
docs.text:
ZigBeeController            needs zigbee/ezsp | znp | deconz | …
├── a Zigbee stick          zigbee/ezsp at /dev/serial/by-id/…
├── or silabs-multiprotocol zigbee/ezsp at socket://127.0.0.1:9999
│   └── a multi-PAN stick   multipan/silabs-cpc
└── or another stick        recognised by the integration's own UsbDriver, e.g. zigbee/znp

The controller reads self.peripherals.endpoint("zigbee") and opens whatever it gets: a serial path or a TCP socket, in the dialect it names. Switching from a Zigbee stick to a multi-PAN one needs no change in its code.

docs.title: Without the Hub
docs.text: The standalone runner binds peripherals the same way, or lets you pass them yourself. See Standalone Mode.

docs.title: Quality Checklist
docs.text:
The Implementation Checklist gets your integration functional — it launches, pairs, controls, and reports. This checklist gets it reliable and maintainable: it's the bar an integration must clear before it's released.

Items are ordered from vital (never ship without them) to nice-to-have.

Track it in your repo, not here

The integration template README ships both checklists as a fillable copy — tick items there as you implement them and your CI goes green. This page is the reference that explains the why behind each item.

docs.title: Reliability — vital
docs.text:
An integration must never take the Hub down, and never spam the logs. The Hub isolates a crashing integration where it can, but a quality integration doesn't rely on that.

  • [ ] Recovers automatically. Connection loss, an offline device, or a restarted backend/radio must recover on their own — no manual restart. Reconnection is retried with backoff, not a tight loop.
  • [ ] No exception escapes the controller. Every background task, subscription loop, and callback catches its own errors. An unhandled exception in a background task dies silently; one raised inside a self.output.* call propagates back into the Hub. Neither is acceptable.
  • [ ] Failures are surfaced, not raised. An expected/transient failure (device offline, bad reading, timeout) is logged once (no repeated spam) and reflected on the device — device.available = False and a human-readable last_error — then cleared on recovery. It does not bubble up as an exception.
  • [ ] Re-authenticates automatically when credentials expire or are rejected (if the protocol uses credentials).
  • [ ] Fully asynchronous. No blocking I/O on the event loop; blocking or CPU-heavy work runs off-loop (a thread/executor) so it can't stall the Hub.
  • [ ] Availability is live. Offline/online is detected while the Hub is running, not only on reboot (this also appears on the implementation checklist — it's a reliability requirement, so it's repeated here).
  • [ ] Stable identity. Device and parameter UUIDs are derived through the SDK helpers, so they stay identical across restarts and re-pairs — state and automations survive.
  • [ ] No environment variables and no device paths. Radios, servers, discovery and options arrive from the Hub. Nothing is read from the environment or hardcoded, so the integration works with whatever stick the user plugs in.
  • [ ] Everything external declared as a Need — radios, BLE_ROUTER, ZEROCONF, UPNP_SSDP, and the companion servers it brings as Services. Never raw Bluetooth (ble/bluez): the router holds every adapter. Optional (BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False)) where the integration still works without it.
  • [ ] Bound needs read from self.peripherals, host facts and storage from self.platform, settings from self.settings, reports through self.output.
  • [ ] Integration-level problems reported with a stable error id (IntegrationError) and resolved when they clear (controller_did_resolve_error), e.g. once the server is back.

docs.title: Tested — vital
docs.text:
• [ ] End-to-end automated tests drive the controller through pair → command → fetch → events → unpair against a virtual/simulated device (the SDK's majordom_integration_sdk.testing doubles), with no physical hardware required.
  • [ ] Failure paths are tested — offline device, transport error, rejected credentials, a failed pairing rolled back by unpair(draft) and then retried, unpair of an unreachable device raising DeviceUnreachableError — asserting the integration degrades gracefully (sets available/last_error, does not raise).
  • [ ] Behaviour without a required radio is tested. Losing the radio or service while running reports an IntegrationError with is_still_running=False, so the Hub restarts the integration, instead of hanging; an unbound optional need doesn't stop it from starting.
  • [ ] Broad device coverage where the protocol has many device/parameter types — exercise the full mapping surface, not one happy-path device. (A protocol-provided virtual-device catalogue, run in CI, is the ideal.)

docs.title: Maintainable — important
docs.text:
• [ ] Fully typed — passes ty with no package-wide ignore blocks; any exceptions are file/rule-scoped and commented with why.
  • [ ] Clean — passes the full poe check (ruff lint + format, ty, tests, build) with no warnings.
  • [ ] Readable & structured — clear names, comments where the intent isn't obvious; conversion logic lives in a mapper and models are separated, per the template layout.
  • [ ] Efficient — prefer event subscriptions over polling; batch or chunk reads; avoid redundant network and CPU work.
  • [ ] Diagnosable — logging at the right levels, enough to debug a device problem from the logs alone. A device-state diagnostic dump is a bonus.
  • [ ] Owned — a listed maintainer who keeps it working as the protocol and the upstream library evolve.

docs.title: User experience — important
docs.text:
• [ ] Settings have plain-language titles. Every settings field has a title (and a description where it helps) written for the user, and a default.
  • [ ] Rich parameter metadata. Every parameter has the correct visibility (user / setting / system) and the device's main parameter is set — so the app can present a clean control-center action, a sensible on-tap parameter list, a settings page, and hidden system internals. Getting this right is what makes a device feel native rather than a raw dump of protocol attributes; a poorly-mapped device is a poor device, however reliable it is.

docs.title: Extras — nice-to-have
docs.text:
• [ ] Logical, localizable naming — device and parameter names read well to a non-technical user and can be translated.
  • [ ] Firmware/software updates — device firmware can be updated through the Hub, where supported. (The update API is still WIP.)
  • [ ] User documentation — a supported-device list, setup notes, and troubleshooting aimed at non-technical users.

docs.title: Reporting errors
docs.text:
The reliability rules above hinge on one habit: catch errors at the edges and turn them into state, not exceptions.

  • Inside a background task or subscription loop, wrap the body in a try/except. On a per-device failure, set that device's available/last_error and keep the loop alive.
  • Never let an exception cross into a self.output.* call — the Hub treats those callbacks as trusted and an exception there can disrupt Hub-side handling.
  • Log an expected failure once at the appropriate level; don't re-log the same condition every poll.

For controller-level problems that aren't tied to a single device (e.g. the backend/radio went away entirely), call controller_did_encounter_error with an IntegrationError — it surfaces a plain-language message to the user until you resolve its id with controller_did_resolve_error, and is_still_running=False marks the whole integration as failed. See Reporting errors to the user.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Give the user options by declaring a pydantic model. The Hub turns it into a form in the app, stores the values, and hands them to your controller.

docs.title: Declaring settings
docs.text:
Declare the model as a nested Settings class, named as the controller's last type parameter:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from majordom_integration_sdk import AbstractController, Device, Parameter
from majordom_integration_sdk import SettingsExtraField as Extra


class AcmeController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter, "AcmeController.Settings"]):
    class Settings(BaseModel):
        poll_interval: int = Field(30, ge=5, le=3600, title="Poll interval, seconds")
        api_token: str = Field("", title="Cloud API token", json_schema_extra={Extra.write_only: True})
        firmware: str | None = Field(None, title="Bridge firmware", json_schema_extra={Extra.read_only: True})

The app builds the form from the model's JSON schema. So:

  • Give every field a title and, where it helps, a description, in plain language for the user: what it is, and what an empty value does.
  • Use pydantic constraints (ge, le, Literal[...]). The Hub validates every change against them.
  • Give every field a default: the Hub creates the settings before the user opens the form.

Mark fields with SettingsExtraField, never a spelled-out keyword:

  • write_only: the user sets it, and the Hub never shows it again (a secret). An update that leaves it out keeps it.
  • read_only: your controller fills it in itself (self.settings.firmware = "2.1"). The user sees it but can't change it. It isn't stored.

docs.title: Reading settings
docs.text: The validated instance is self.settings, typed by your model. Without a Settings class, it is NoSettings.

docs.title: Defaults are kept
docs.text:
The Hub stores the values the first time it reads the settings, defaults included. A default_factory runs once, and its result stays: that's how to generate a secret once per Hub, e.g. network keys.

api_secret: str = Field(default_factory=lambda: secrets.token_hex(16), title="Secret", json_schema_extra={Extra.write_only: True})

It also means a default you change in a later release applies to new Hubs only.

docs.title: Settings of a service
docs.text:
A Service can have settings too. Pass the model as settings=, and use its fields in compose as {settings.<field>}:

class ServerOptions(BaseModel):
    log_level: Literal["info", "debug"] = Field("info", title="Server log level")


Service(
    "acme-server",
    compose={"image": "…", "environment": {"LOG_LEVEL": "{settings.log_level}"}},
    settings=ServerOptions,
)

The user sees a service's settings next to the settings of every integration that uses it.

docs.title: Changing settings
docs.text:
The user changes settings in the app; the Hub validates and stores them, then applies them. A service is recreated. Your controller gets settings_did_change(before): return True when you applied them in place, or leave the default (False) to be restarted.

In standalone mode, pass them to the constructor, AcmeController(platform, settings=AcmeController.Settings(poll_interval=10)), or change them through the runtime: await runtime.update_settings(runtime.peripheral("acme"), {"poll_interval": 10}).

docs.title: Hub settings
docs.text:
Some settings belong to the whole Hub. They reach you as facts on self.platform (and {platform.<fact>} in a service's compose):

Fact Meaning platform.region where the Hub is used, for sub-GHz radios, named as Z-Wave JS names them: Europe, USA, … platform.wifi the Wi-Fi network to set new devices up on (ssid, password), or None platform.thread_dataset the active dataset of the Hub's Thread network, hex; learned from the border router, not set by the user

When they change, your controller gets platform_facts_did_change(before). Read self.platform each time you need a fact: a platform object you kept holds the old values.

docs.title: Standalone Mode — Running an Integration Without the Hub
docs.text:
Every MajorDom integration is a self-contained library for its protocol. The Hub is just one consumer: it calls your package's peripherals(platform), binds their needs, and drives them. You can do exactly the same thing yourself — to script a device, embed an integration in another app, or test against real hardware — with no Hub involved.

There are three ways to run one, all in majordom_integration_sdk.dev:

run_cli(...) run_controller(...) build_platform(...) Use for driving a device by hand from a prompt watching devices, quick demos programmatic pair / control / fetch Needs bound by the runtime, as under the Hub bound by the runtime you hand over Peripherals, or drive a Runner Output interactive commands + console log logs discoveries/events to the console your delegate (see below) Blocks interactive prompt until exit runs until Ctrl-C you drive the lifecycle Extra deps [cli], plus the runtime's [runtime,ble,discovery] none

run_cli and run_controller start the SDK runtime for the controller, as the Hub does: the Bluetooth router over the local adapters, Zeroconf, SSDP, the radios it finds and the services it runs in Docker (default_peripherals()). The controller starts once its required needs are bound, stops when one is lost, and hears about moved peripherals, settings and platform facts through its hooks, restarting unless they handle them. The runtime needs its extras:

pip install "majordom-integration-sdk[runtime,ble,discovery]"

Without them, the runner stops with that install hint, or pass peripherals={...} yourself (see below).

docs.title: Interactive CLI — run_cli
docs.text:
The fastest way to actually use an integration by hand: it starts the controller under the runtime with a local device store, then drops you into a prompt to pair, control, and inspect devices, and to see or pin what its needs are bound to. It's the MajorDom Hub's operator CLI, scoped to a single integration.

The interactive CLI needs one more extra (typer-shell + rich), so install the cli extra too:

pip install "majordom-integration-sdk[cli,runtime,ble,discovery]"

# cli.py
import asyncio
from uuid import uuid4
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import run_cli
import integration_template  # your integration

asyncio.run(run_cli(integration_template.peripherals, db_path="devices.db"))

python cli.py

example > help          # list commands
example > discoveries   # devices seen on the network (id, name, transport, expected credentials)
example > pair <discovery_id> [credentials_type] [credentials_value]
example > pair_window 60 # open a join window (Zigbee); no-op where discovery is continuous
example > devices        # paired devices (id, name, available)
example > device <id>    # its parameters (id, name, role, visibility, value)
example > control <physical_id> <parameter_id> <value>   # value parsed as JSON if possible
example > identify <physical_id>   # blink/beep
example > fetch <physical_id>      # refresh state from the device
example > unpair <physical_id>
example > needs          # each need: what it is bound to and by whom, or why it isn't bound
example > pin <family> <url> [dialect]   # provide an endpoint yourself, e.g. pin zigbee socket://192.168.1.5:6638 ezsp
example > unpin <family>  # drop it: the runtime binds the need again
example > resolve        # look for radios again and bind every need anew
example > exit

needs prints one line per need:

zigbee/ezsp|znp|deconz|…  -> /dev/serial/by-id/usb-…  by usb-…
ble/router (optional)  -> router  by ble-router
thread/otbr-rest (optional)  unbound: need thread/otbr-rest: nothing offers it

pin takes the need's first dialect when you give none (pin matter ws://127.0.0.1:5580); its endpoint is shared and wins over anything the runtime finds. pin, unpin and resolve need the runtime: with peripherals= given by hand they raise.

Pass db_path= to keep paired devices across restarts (a file-backed store); omit it for an in-memory one. Under the hood this is exactly the wiring described below — the same build_platform and runtime plus a delegate that persists state — so anything the CLI does you can also do in code.

docs.title: Watch mode — run_controller
docs.text:
The quickest way to see an integration work. It starts the runtime for your controller, a file-backed device store, and a console logger, then runs your controller until interrupted:

import asyncio
from uuid import uuid4
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import run_controller
import integration_template  # your integration

asyncio.run(run_controller(integration_template.peripherals, db_path="devices.db"))

A need that stays unbound is logged with its reason, e.g. ble isn't bound: need ble/bluez: every provider taken by ble-router — use Need("ble", ["router"]).

docs.title: Programmatic mode — build the platform, call the controller
docs.text:
For anything beyond watching — pair a device, send a command, fetch state — build the platform yourself and call the controller's methods directly (library mode):

import asyncio
from uuid import uuid4
from majordom_integration_sdk import Endpoint, Peripherals
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import build_platform
from integration_template.controller import ExampleController

async def main():
    controller = ExampleController(build_platform(db_path="devices.db"))
    controller.peripherals = Peripherals({"example": Endpoint("example", "echo", "tcp://127.0.0.1:7000")})
    controller.output = MyDelegate()  # see below; logs by default
    await controller.start()
    # ... await controller.pair_device(discovery, draft, ProvidedCredentials(...)), save it, fetch, send_command ...
    await controller.stop()

asyncio.run(main())

To have the runtime bind the needs instead, use build_runtime and a Runner, as run_controller does:

from pathlib import Path
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import Runner, build_platform, build_runtime

platform = build_platform()
exported = integration_template.peripherals(platform)
controller = next(p for p in exported if isinstance(p, ExampleController))
runner = Runner(controller, build_runtime(exported, Path(".majordom-dev/runtime"), platform=platform))
await runner.start()  # starts the runtime; the controller starts once its required needs are bound
...
await runner.stop()

docs.title: Connecting to radios and services
docs.text:
An integration with needs gets its peripherals from the runtime, standalone as under the Hub. How much of it runs is up to you:

Level You run The runtime runs Pass Full nothing default_peripherals(): providers, radios, services in Docker nothing Partial some of it, e.g. your own border router or no Docker what you list pinned=[...], runtime_peripherals=[...] Bare the radio or server nothing (library mode) peripherals={...}

docs.title: Full: everything automatic
docs.text:
asyncio.run(run_controller(majordom_zigbee.peripherals))

The runtime finds sticks, identifies them, binds every need, runs the services, and keeps watching. It keeps its state and the services' data in .majordom-dev/runtime (under storage_root=). Services need Docker, and recognising Silicon Labs sticks needs the universal-silabs-flasher command on PATH.

docs.title: Partial: no Docker, no radios, your own servers
docs.text:
On a machine without Docker or radios, run only the peripherals you want and pin what you run yourself. A pinned endpoint wins over anything the runtime finds, and no container starts for a need it serves:

import asyncio
from uuid import uuid4
import majordom_zwave
from majordom_integration_sdk import Endpoint
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import run_controller
from majordom_integration_sdk.runtime import HostNetwork

asyncio.run(run_controller(
    majordom_zwave.peripherals,
    runtime_peripherals=[HostNetwork()],  # no USB scanning, no Docker
    pinned=[Endpoint("zwave", "zwave-js-ws", "ws://localhost:3000")],  # your zwave-js-server
))

Pin thread (Endpoint("thread", "otbr-rest", "http://my-otbr:8081", is_shared=True)) to keep matterjs-server running here, but behind your border router. In the CLI, pin and unpin do the same while it runs.

Under the runtime, settings come from it, as under the Hub: change them with runtime.update_settings(peripheral, values) (see Settings). Platform facts are keyword arguments: run_controller(..., region="Europe").

docs.title: Bare: pass the peripherals yourself
docs.text:
You already have the stick or the server, or don't want the runtime at all. Hand the controller its peripherals; the runtime doesn't start, and nothing is bound or rebound:

asyncio.run(run_controller(
    majordom_zigbee.peripherals,
    peripherals={"zigbee": Endpoint("zigbee", "ezsp", "/dev/ttyUSB0")},
))

run_controller and run_cli also take any field of Platform as a keyword argument, e.g. wifi=WifiCredentials("Home", "password"), the network to commission devices onto.

A typed need for Zeroconf, SSDP or the router then takes an instance you start yourself, as Endpoint("mdns", "zeroconf", instance=zeroconf). You run the servers here: restart them yourself; the controller reconnects on its own.

docs.title: The runtime as a library
docs.text:
The runner wraps majordom_integration_sdk.runtime.Runtime, which you can also drive yourself, for several integrations at once. It runs peripherals in the order given:

from pathlib import Path
from majordom_integration_sdk import Endpoint
from majordom_integration_sdk.runtime import Pinned, Runtime, default_peripherals

platform = build_platform()
runtime = Runtime(
    Path("runtime"),  # where it keeps its state and the services' data
    [
        Pinned(Endpoint("zwave", "zwave-js-ws", "ws://my-zwave:3000")),
        *default_peripherals(),
        *majordom_matter.peripherals(platform),
        *majordom_zwave.peripherals(platform),
    ],
    platform=platform,
)
await runtime.start()  # starts what is wanted, binds, runs services, keeps watching
matter = runtime.peripheral("matter")
runtime.bound(matter)  # {"matter": Endpoint("matter", "matter-server", "ws://127.0.0.1:5580"), …}
runtime.unbound(matter)  # why each unbound need isn't bound, by family
Call Does peripheral(key), peripherals() one peripheral by its key; every one, in binding order status(p) its state (waiting, running, failed, …) and why bound(p), unbound(p), providers(p) what its needs are bound to, why not, and by whom enable(p), disable(p), restart(p) the user's switches; DisabledStore keeps them by key update_settings(p, values) validate, store and apply new settings update_platform(platform) new platform facts, handed to every peripheral refresh() look for radios again and bind anew

Pass output= (a RuntimeOutput) to hear about every change of status and what peripherals learn.

docs.title: The platform
docs.text:
build_platform() returns a Platform like the Hub's: frozen, the same for every peripheral.

  • device_repository(p) — one unit of work on the device store, scoped to the peripheral's key. db_path= selects a file-backed SQLite repository; omit it for an in-memory one.
  • documents_folder(p) — a folder per peripheral key under storage_root (.majordom-dev).
  • region, wifi, thread_dataset — the host's facts; set them with dataclasses.replace(platform, region="Europe").

The controller's output, settings and needs are not on the platform: they are self.output, self.settings and self.peripherals.

docs.title: Receiving discoveries & events — implement a delegate
docs.text:
The controller doesn't return discoveries and events; it pushes them to self.output. To act on them in standalone mode, pass an object implementing the ControllerOutput protocol. The simplest path is to subclass the SDK's LoggingControllerOutput and override only what you need:

import asyncio
from uuid import uuid4
from majordom_integration_sdk.dev import LoggingControllerOutput, build_platform
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.credentials import CredentialsType, ProvidedCredentials
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.device import DeviceState
from integration_template.controller import ExampleController

class MyDelegate(LoggingControllerOutput):
    def __init__(self):
        self.discoveries = {}

    async def controller_did_receive_discovery(self, controller, discovery):
        self.discoveries[discovery.id] = discovery

    async def controller_did_receive_events(self, controller, events):
        for event in events:
            print("event:", event)

async def main():
    delegate = MyDelegate()
    controller = ExampleController(build_platform(db_path="devices.db"))
    controller.peripherals = peripherals  # bound by hand, or drive it through a Runner
    controller.output = delegate
    await controller.start()

    # wait for the first discovery, then pair it
    while not delegate.discoveries:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    discovery = next(iter(delegate.discoveries.values()))
    # no Hub here: build the draft it would build, pair, then save and fetch as it does
    draft = DeviceState(id=discovery.id, name=discovery.device_name, room_id=uuid4(), transport=discovery.transport,
                        integration=controller.key, manufacturer=discovery.device_manufacturer, parameters=[])
    device = await controller.pair_device(
        discovery, draft, ProvidedCredentials(type=CredentialsType.code, value="123-45-678")
    )
    async with controller.platform.device_repository(controller) as repo:
        await repo.save(device)
        if read := await controller.fetch(device):  # None: it didn't answer
            await repo.save(read)

    # ... controller.send_command(...), controller.identify(device) ...

    await controller.stop()

asyncio.run(main())

The full delegate surface — every method the controller may call:

Method Called when controller_did_receive_discovery(controller, discovery) a new device is discovered controller_did_update_discovery(controller, discovery) a known discovery's details change controller_did_lose_discovery(controller, discovery_id) a discovery is gone controller_did_connect_device(controller, *, physical_id) a paired device comes online (incl. after pairing) controller_did_lose_device(controller, *, physical_id) a paired device goes offline controller_did_receive_events(controller, events) the device reports parameter changes (DeviceParameterChange) controller_did_encounter_error(controller, error) / controller_did_resolve_error(controller, error_id) an IntegrationError is active / gone controller_did_emit_notification(controller, notification) a user-facing notification controller_did_change_provided(controller) what it provides changed (the runtime takes this one)

Subclassing LoggingControllerOutput gives every method a logging default, so you only implement the ones you care about.

docs.title: Testing without real devices
docs.text: For tests, prefer the offline doubles in majordom_integration_sdk.testing — build_test_platform() (in-memory repository, temp-dir storage) plus RecordingControllerOutput (captures discoveries/events for assertions), and FakeZeroconf, FakeSSDP, FakeBLERouter with FakeBLESources, FakeCompose and FakePeripheral for the peripherals — over build_platform and real hardware. See Example Integration and any integration's tests/.

docs.title: integration_data
docs.text:
MajorDom's Device and Parameter schemas expose an integration_data field for storing protocol-specific state (pairing tokens, internal IDs, etc.). By default it is an untyped dict persisted as JSON.

Integrations can subclass Device/DeviceState and Parameter/ParameterState to declare a typed schema for that field — Hub will then handle (de-)serialization automatically before passing Device instance to Controller's methods or when saving to the database.

# majordom_myintegration/models.py
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.base import Base
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.device import Device, DeviceState
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas.parameter import Parameter, ParameterState

class MyDeviceIntegrationData(Base):
    pairing_token: str | None = None

class MyDevice(Device):
    integration_data: MyDeviceIntegrationData

class MyParameterState(ParameterState):
    integration_data: MyParameterIntegrationData

To make the Hub use these custom types, the integration's Controller must override device_type and parameter_type:

@property
def device_type(self) -> type[MyDevice]:
    return MyDevice

@property
def parameter_type(self) -> type[MyParameter]:
    return MyParameter

The Hub will deserialize objects into these types before passing them to your implemented methods.

The draft that pair_device fills is a DeviceState. To give it your own integration_data schema, subclass DeviceState and override device_state_type the same way. The Hub validates the draft into it:

@property
def device_state_type(self) -> type[MyDeviceState]:
    return MyDeviceState

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
Use self.platform.device_repository(self), scoped to your integration's key, to read or persist devices. Not in pair_device: it fills the draft and returns it, and the Hub saves it (see Pairing). Use the repository everywhere else, for example to update a paired device later:

async with self.platform.device_repository(self) as repo:
    device = await repo.get(physical_id=physical_id, as_=MyDevice) # `as_=MyDevice` is optional but provides hassle-free deserialization

async with self.platform.device_repository(self) as repo:
    device.integration_data.some_field = new_value # assuming `MyDevice.integration_data` uses custom class with `some_field` present
    await repo.save(device)

docs.title: File Storage (documents_folder)
docs.text:
For files that cannot be stored in the database (e.g. a protocol's own SQLite DB, certificates, binary blobs), use self.platform.documents_folder(self):

path = self.platform.documents_folder(self) / "zigbee.db"

Resolves to a directory for this integration's key under the Hub's data root, created on use. For JSON files, majordom_integration_sdk.files.read_json / write_json write whole or not at all, readable by the owner only (0600): use them for anything holding secrets.

docs.title: Bluetooth LE
docs.text: Everything an integration does over Bluetooth goes through one object: the BLERouter.

docs.title: What the router is
docs.text:
The Hub may have several Bluetooth radios: its own adapter, a USB dongle, the Bluetooth of a multi-PAN stick, and ESPHome nodes acting as Bluetooth proxies around the house. The router holds all of them and gives every integration one API:

  • Discovery: you say which devices you want to hear about, and it reports them, whichever radio heard them.
  • Connections: you connect by address, and it picks the radio that hears the device best.
  • Leases: you lock one radio to one device for a long setup, while the others keep working for everyone.

Your code never knows which radio carries a connection. A device in the garage reached through an ESPHome proxy works the same as one next to the Hub.

Never access Bluetooth hardware directly

Don't open adapters, scan or connect with bleak, BlueZ, bluetoothctl or any other library or service. The router already holds every radio: a direct scan competes with it, misses the proxies, and can break another integration's pairing. A need for raw Bluetooth (Need("ble", ["bluez"])) is never bound while the router runs.

docs.title: Getting the router
docs.text:
Need BLE_ROUTER, and read it from self.peripherals:

from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLE_ROUTER


class AcmeController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    needs = [BLE_ROUTER]

    async def start(self):
        self._ble = self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER)

When the integration also works without Bluetooth, make the need optional. instance() then returns None on a hub without Bluetooth:

needs = [BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False)]

docs.title: Discovering devices
docs.text:
See Bluetooth Discovery: router.register(listener, matchers), with a full example.

router.devices() returns every device heard recently, if you need a snapshot instead of events.

docs.title: Connecting and using GATT
docs.text:
connect(address) opens a GATT connection for the block, and closes it when the block ends. Characteristics are addressed by their handle, which you find in services():

BATTERY_LEVEL = "00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"


async def read_battery(self, address: str) -> int:
    async with self._ble.connect(address) as connection:
        characteristics = [c for s in await connection.services() for c in s.characteristics]
        battery = next(c for c in characteristics if c.uuid == BATTERY_LEVEL)
        return (await connection.read(battery.handle))[0]
BLEConnection Does await connection.services() the device's GATT services, each with its characteristics (uuid, handle, properties) await connection.read(handle) reads a characteristic, as bytes await connection.write(handle, data, is_response_needed=True) writes a characteristic; False for "write without response" await connection.start_notify(handle, callback) calls callback(data) on every notification or indication await connection.stop_notify(handle) stops them await connection.disconnect() closes the connection before the block ends connection.mtu the negotiated MTU, to size your packets connect(…) parameter Meaning on_disconnect called when the connection drops busy_timeout seconds to reach the device, waiting for a radio leased to someone else (default 10). Then BLEBusyError when every radio that hears it is still leased, or ConnectionError (which BLEBusyError also is) when none reaches it max_duration seconds after which the connection is closed and the block gets TimeoutError (default 600); None keeps it open, only when you mean it

Every Bluetooth radio has only a few connection slots, a proxy fewer still: keep the block short. When a connection must outlive a block, like a subscription kept while the integration runs, open_connection(…, max_duration=None) takes the same parameters and returns the connection: disconnect it yourself.

docs.title: Locking a radio: exclusive
docs.text:
A short exchange (read a value, send a command) just connects. A long, multi-step setup should lease the radio first, so nobody else's connection or scan disrupts the operation:

from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLEBusyError

try:
    async with self._ble.exclusive(address, owner=self.key, max_duration=300) as lease, lease.connect() as connection:
        await self._provision(connection)  # several reads, writes and notifications
except BLEBusyError:
    ...  # tell the user the Hub's Bluetooth is busy, try again later

While the block runs, the radio that hears the device best stops scanning and serves only you; the other radios keep working for everyone. When the block ends, the radio goes back to the router. Always connect through lease.connect(), not self._ble.connect(), inside the block; it takes the same parameters.

Lock Don't lock Commissioning or pairing that takes several steps (Matter commissioning, Wi-Fi provisioning over Improv) Discovery: the router does it for you A firmware update Reading a value or sending a command Anything that must not lose its radio halfway Anything over in a second or two

A lease blocks other integrations from that radio, so hold it no longer than the setup takes.

Parameter Meaning owner who holds it, for the logs: your integration's key busy_timeout seconds to wait for a free radio before BLEBusyError (default 30) max_duration seconds the lease holds the radio; then the block gets TimeoutError and the radio goes back (default 120) wait seconds to wait for the best radio before trying the next one (default 1) is_pairing_needed lease only a radio that can pair (see below); BLEPairingError when none hears the device

docs.title: Pairing and sending credentials
docs.text:
Send credentials (a Wi-Fi password, a Thread network key) only over a secured link. Pick a SecureChannel and open it on the leased connection:

from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLEPairingError, LESecureConnections

channel = LESecureConnections()
async with self._ble.exclusive(address, owner=self.key, is_pairing_needed=channel.is_pairing_needed) as lease:
    async with lease.connect() as connection, channel.secure(connection) as secured:
        await secured.write(credentials_handle, credentials)
Channel Use for LESecureConnections() the default: pairs ("Just Works") before anything is written, and unpairs when the block ends; LESecureConnections(is_pairing_kept=True) keeps the bond. Raises BLEPairingError when the link can't be encrypted, so nothing is sent unencrypted Unsecured() firmware that can't pair at all; chosen explicitly, it logs a warning

Not every radio can pair: a source says it can with is_pairable. is_pairing_needed=True leases one that can.

docs.title: Adding a BLE proxy
docs.text:
If your integration talks to devices that have a Bluetooth radio of their own (like ESPHome nodes with bluetooth_proxy), it can lend that radio to the router. Every integration then reaches Bluetooth devices through it.

  1. Implement BLESource for the radio:

    from collections.abc import Callable

from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLEConnection, GattService, OnAdvertisement


class AcmeBLESource:
    name = "acme-1"  # unique: e.g. the radio's MAC
    is_pairable = False  # True when its connections can pair
    free_slots: int | None = 3  # connections it can still open; None when unknown

    async def start(self, on_advertisement: OnAdvertisement): ...  # call on_advertisement(device, advertisement) for each one heard
    async def stop(self): ...
    async def connect(self, address: str, on_disconnect: Callable[[], None]) -> BLEConnection:
        return AcmeBLEConnection(await self._radio.connect(address), on_disconnect)  # pseudo


class AcmeBLEConnection:
    """Wraps one GATT connection of the radio: the router hands it to integrations as a `BLEConnection`."""

    mtu: int

    async def services(self) -> list[GattService]: ...
    async def read(self, handle: int) -> bytes: ...
    async def write(self, handle: int, data: bytes, is_response_needed: bool = True): ...
    async def start_notify(self, handle: int, callback: Callable[[bytes], None]): ...
    async def stop_notify(self, handle: int): ...
    async def disconnect(self): ...  # call on_disconnect() when the radio reports the link dropped, too

    A radio whose connections can pair returns PairableBLEConnections (with pair() and unpair()) and sets is_pairable = True.

    A source that can stop scanning without letting go of its radio also implements pause_scanning() and resume_scanning(); one that can switch to active scanning implements set_scan_mode(is_active). The router uses them when they are there.

  2. Provide it as a BLEProxy while the radio is reachable, and tell the Hub each time that changes:

    from majordom_integration_sdk.peripherals import BLEProxy


class AcmeController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    @property
    def provides(self) -> list[BLEProxy]:
        return list(self._proxies.values())

    async def _on_node_connected(self, node_id: str, source: AcmeBLESource):
        self._proxies[node_id] = BLEProxy(source)
        await self.output.controller_did_change_provided(self)

    async def _on_node_lost(self, node_id: str):
        if self._proxies.pop(node_id, None):
            await self.output.controller_did_change_provided(self)

Keep BLEProxy's default dialect: the router hears through proxies as ble/esphome-proxy, whoever brings them. It starts hearing through the proxy at once, and lets it go when you take it back or the integration stops. See Peripherals for providing peripherals in general.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The SDK's test doubles (the ble extra) run a real router over fake radios:

from majordom_integration_sdk import Peripherals
from majordom_integration_sdk.testing import FakeBLERouter, FakeBLESource, build_test_platform

radio = FakeBLESource("hci0", connection=my_fake_connection, is_pairable=True)
router = FakeBLERouter(sources=[radio])
await router.start()

controller = AcmeController(build_test_platform())
controller.peripherals = Peripherals({"ble": router.endpoint})
await controller.start()

radio.advertise("AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF", local_name="Acme", service_uuids=["0000fd00-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"])

To test a proxy you provide, hand its source to the router: await router.add_source(controller.provides[0].source).

docs.title: Discovery Services
docs.text:
Discovery services tell your controller when devices appear, change or go away, over mDNS, SSDP or Bluetooth. Need them by the SDK's typed needs (majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities) and read the bound one with self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF). They share one listener pattern, and your integration never runs its own mDNS, SSDP or BLE scanner.

Three are available:

Capability Need Contract Protocol mdns/zeroconf ZEROCONF Zeroconf mDNS / DNS-SD upnp/ssdp UPNP_SSDP SSDP UPnP SSDP ble/router BLE_ROUTER BLERouter Bluetooth Low Energy, through every radio the hub has; for everything else over BLE see Bluetooth LE

The contracts (interfaces and info types only) live in majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities. See Peripherals for needs in general.

docs.title: Common Pattern
docs.text:
All three services share the same usage contract:

  • Call register(...) to subscribe. It returns a cancel closure.
  • Store the cancel closure and call it in your controller's stop().
  • The runtime starts and stops them — do not call start() or stop() on them yourself.
  • Make the need optional, BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False), when the integration works without it: a hub without Bluetooth then still runs it, with instance(BLE_ROUTER) returning None.

docs.title: Combining Multiple Discovery Services
docs.text:
A controller can register with multiple discovery protocols simultaneously, or with a few service types using the same protocol. Usage doesn't change.

from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLE_ROUTER, ZEROCONF

needs = [ZEROCONF, BLE_ROUTER]

async def start(self):
    self._cancels: set[Callable[[], None]] = set()
    self._cancels.add(self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF).register(
        self, {"_myprotocol._tcp.local."}
    ))
    self._cancels.add(self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER).register(
        self, {MY_SERVICE_UUID}
    ))

async def stop(self):
    for cancel in self._cancels:
        cancel()

docs.title: Bluetooth (BLE) Discovery
docs.text:
Never access Bluetooth hardware directly

Never access Bluetooth hardware directly via bluez, bleak or other Python libraries, system services, or any other way. For Bluetooth discovery, always use BLERouter as described below. For the full BLE specification with other usage, e.g. pairing and controlling devices, see Capabilities: Bluetooth LE.

The router hears every Bluetooth radio the hub has. You tell it which devices you are interested in, and it calls your controller when one appears, changes its advertisement, or goes away.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Everything a controller needs for BLE discovery. Copy it and change the three numbered lines:

from uuid import UUID

from majordom_integration_sdk import AbstractController, Device, Discovery, Parameter, Platform
from majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities import BLE_ROUTER, BLEDiscoveryInfo, BLEMatcher, BLERouter
from majordom_integration_sdk.schemas import CredentialsOption, CredentialsType

# 1. Which devices to hear about: here, everything advertising this service UUID
MATCHERS = [BLEMatcher(service_uuid=UUID("0000fd00-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"))]


class AcmeController(AbstractController[Device, Parameter]):
    needs = [BLE_ROUTER]  # the Hub hands the router over in self.peripherals

    def __init__(self, platform: Platform, *, settings=None):
        super().__init__(platform, settings=settings)
        self._discoveries: dict[UUID, Discovery] = {}

    async def start(self):
        ble = self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER)
        self._cancel_ble = ble.register(self, MATCHERS)

    async def stop(self):
        self._cancel_ble()

    @property
    def discoveries(self) -> dict[UUID, Discovery]:
        return self._discoveries.copy()

    # BLEDiscoveryListener: called by the router

    async def ble_did_discover_device(self, ble: BLERouter, info: BLEDiscoveryInfo):
        discovery = self._to_discovery(info)
        self._discoveries[discovery.id] = discovery
        await self.output.controller_did_receive_discovery(self, discovery)

    async def ble_did_update_device(self, ble: BLERouter, info: BLEDiscoveryInfo):
        discovery = self._to_discovery(info)
        self._discoveries[discovery.id] = discovery
        await self.output.controller_did_update_discovery(self, discovery)

    async def ble_did_remove_device(self, ble: BLERouter, info: BLEDiscoveryInfo):
        discovery_id = self._discovery_id(info)
        if self._discoveries.pop(discovery_id, None):
            await self.output.controller_did_lose_discovery(self, discovery_id)

    def _discovery_id(self, info: BLEDiscoveryInfo) -> UUID:
        # 2. A stable id from the advertisement's content, e.g. a serial number in the manufacturer data
        serial = info.advertisement.manufacturer_data[0xFFFF].hex()
        return self.device_uuid(serial)

    def _to_discovery(self, info: BLEDiscoveryInfo) -> Discovery:
        return Discovery(
            id=self._discovery_id(info),
            integration=self.key,
            expected_credentials_options=[CredentialsOption(type=CredentialsType.none)],
            transport="BLE",
            device_manufacturer="Acme",  # 3. What the user sees
            device_name=info.advertisement.local_name or "Acme sensor",
            device_category=None,
            device_icon=None,
        )

    # pair_device, send_command and the rest: see Implementing a Controller

Don't build ids from the address

Many devices rotate their Bluetooth address, and each radio may report a different one. Derive the discovery id from the advertisement's content: a serial number, a MAC address inside the manufacturer data, Matter's discriminator with its vendor and product ids.

If your integration also works without Bluetooth, make the need optional and check for None:

needs = [BLE_ROUTER(is_required=False)]

async def start(self):
    ble = self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER)  # None on a hub without Bluetooth
    self._cancel_ble = ble.register(self, MATCHERS) if ble else None

docs.title: Matchers
docs.text:
A listener hears about a device when it matches any of its matchers. A plain UUID matches that service. In a BLEMatcher, every field that is set must match:

Field Matches service_uuid a service UUID, advertised as a service or in the service data service_data_uuid a UUID in the service data only manufacturer_id a company id in the manufacturer data, e.g. 0x004C for Apple manufacturer_data_start the first bytes of that manufacturer data (with manufacturer_id) local_name_prefix the start of the advertised name

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Callback Called when ble_did_discover_device a matching device is heard for the first time; devices heard before you registered count as new ble_did_update_device its advertisement changed (name, service UUIDs, manufacturer or service data); signal strength alone doesn't count ble_did_remove_device no radio has heard it for about 11 seconds

info.device is bleak's BLEDevice (.address, .name); info.advertisement is bleak's AdvertisementData; info.rssi is the signal of the radio that hears it best.

To connect to a discovered device, see Capabilities: Bluetooth LE.

docs.title: Active scanning in a pairing window
docs.text:
Radios scan passively: they hear every advertisement, but many devices send their name only when asked. While the user is pairing, ask for an active scan:

async def start_pairing_window(self, duration_sec: int, credentials: ProvidedCredentials | None = None):
    await self.peripherals.instance(BLE_ROUTER).scan_actively(duration_sec)

docs.title: SSDP
docs.text: The upnp/ssdp peripheral. Declare UPNP_SSDP, and the runtime's listener (SSDPDiscoveryService) arrives as self.peripherals.instance(UPNP_SSDP). Its contract is majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities.SSDP.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
def register(
    self,
    listener: SSDPDiscoveryListener,
    search_target: str,
    mcast_group: str = "239.255.255.250",
    port: int = 1900,
) -> Callable[[], None]: ...
Arg Type Default Description listener SSDPDiscoveryListener required Receives discovery events. search_target str required SSDP ST field. See common templates below. mcast_group str "239.255.255.250" Multicast group. Change only if necessary. port int 1900 SSDP port. Change only if necessary.

Returns a cancel closure — call it in stop() to deregister.

Common search_target values:

ST Discovers "upnp:rootdevice" All UPnP root devices "ssdp:all" All UPnP devices and services "urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaServer:1" UPnP MediaServer devices "uuid:<device-UUID>" A specific device by UUID

docs.title: SSDPDiscoveryListener (Protocol)
docs.text:
class SSDPDiscoveryListener(Protocol):
    async def ssdp_did_discover_service(self, ssdp: SSDP, info: SSDPDiscoveryInfo): ...
    async def ssdp_did_update_service(self, ssdp: SSDP, info: SSDPDiscoveryInfo): ...
    async def ssdp_did_remove_service(self, ssdp: SSDP, info: SSDPDiscoveryInfo): ...

ssdp_did_remove_service fires when a device sends a ssdp:byebye NOTIFY, or when a device fails to respond to several consecutive M-SEARCH bursts (controlled by _missed_scans_evict, default 3 missed scans).

docs.title: SSDPDiscoveryInfo
docs.text:
@dataclass
class SSDPDiscoveryInfo:
    addr: str
    host: str | None
    search_target: str | None
    service_name: str | None        # USN (Unique Service Name)
    server: str | None
    cache_control: str | None
    location: str | None            # URL to the device description XML
    response: dict[str, str]        # full raw response headers

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# in Controller
...
async def start(self):
    self._cancels: set[Callable[[], None]] = set()
    cancel = self.peripherals.instance(UPNP_SSDP).register(
        self,  # self implements SSDPDiscoveryListener
        "urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaServer:1",
    )
    self._cancels.add(cancel)

async def stop(self):
    for cancel in self._cancels:
        cancel()

# SSDPDiscoveryListener Implementation

async def ssdp_did_discover_service(self, ssdp: SSDP, info: SSDPDiscoveryInfo):
    if discovery := self._mapper.map_to_discovery(info):
        self._discoveries[discovery.id] = discovery
        await self.output.controller_did_receive_discovery(self, discovery)

async def ssdp_did_update_service(self, ssdp: SSDP, info: SSDPDiscoveryInfo):
    if discovery := self._mapper.map_to_discovery(info):
        self._discoveries[discovery.id] = discovery
        await self.output.controller_did_update_discovery(self, discovery)

async def ssdp_did_remove_service(self, ssdp: SSDP, info: SSDPDiscoveryInfo):
    discovery_id = self.device_uuid(info.service_name or info.addr)
    if discovery_id in self._discoveries:
        self._discoveries.pop(discovery_id)
        await self.output.controller_did_lose_discovery(self, discovery_id)

docs.title: Zeroconf
docs.text: The mdns/zeroconf peripheral. Declare ZEROCONF, and the runtime's browser (ZeroconfDiscoveryService, the SDK's discovery extra) arrives as self.peripherals.instance(ZEROCONF). Its contract is majordom_integration_sdk.capabilities.Zeroconf.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
def register(
    listener: ZeroconfDiscoveryListener,
    services: set[str],
) -> Callable[[], None]: ...
Arg Type Description listener ZeroconfDiscoveryListener Receives discovery events services set[str] Fully-qualified mDNS service type strings, e.g. "_hap._tcp.local."

Returns a cancel closure — call it in stop() to deregister.

docs.title: async_zeroconf
docs.text:
async_zeroconf: AsyncZeroconf | None

The underlying AsyncZeroconf instance; None until it starts. Use only when you need low-level zeroconf access, or a library takes one (aiohomekit).

docs.title: ZeroconfDiscoveryListener (Protocol)
docs.text:
class ZeroconfDiscoveryListener(Protocol):
    async def zeroconf_did_discover_service(
        self,
        zeroconf: Zeroconf,
        info: ZeroconfDiscoveryInfo,
    ): ...

    async def zeroconf_did_update_service(
        self,
        zeroconf: Zeroconf,
        info: ZeroconfDiscoveryInfo,
    ): ...

    async def zeroconf_did_remove_service(
        self,
        zeroconf: Zeroconf,
        type_: str,
        name: str,
    ): ...

Note: zeroconf_did_remove_service fires on mDNS goodbye packets (TTL=0) or when a silent departure is confirmed: A/AAAA records expired and a follow-up probe got no response. Typical latency for silent departures is ~120 s (A/AAAA TTL). For faster detection, implement liveness checks at the pairing/connection layer.
